rc-p1.title: Passage 1
rc-p1.markdown:
Beneath most forests, the roots of trees are colonized by mycorrhizal fungi, organisms that supply their hosts with water and mineral nutrients in exchange for sugars produced by photosynthesis. Because a single fungus can colonize the roots of several trees at once, its filaments may physically link neighboring plants into what are called common mycorrhizal networks. That such networks exist is not in dispute. What has become contentious is the claim, popularized over the past three decades, that trees use these networks to share resources on a scale that matters ecologically: that large, old trees nourish shaded seedlings through fungal conduits, and even that they preferentially support their own offspring.

The claim rests on a small number of influential experiments. In the best known, researchers exposed one tree to carbon dioxide labeled with a rare isotope of carbon and later detected the isotope in the tissues of a neighboring tree. The result was widely taken to show that carbon had traveled from one plant to the other through the fungal network. Yet the experiment admits of other readings. Labeled carbon can move through the soil itself, released by roots and absorbed by neighbors without any fungal intermediary, and the quantities detected were in most cases small relative to what a seedling fixes through its own photosynthesis. Moreover, carbon found in the fungal tissue sheathing a seedling's roots is not necessarily carbon that the seedling itself can use.

Ecologists who have reviewed the field studies argue that the evidence for network-mediated benefits to seedlings is far thinner than its reputation suggests. In experiments that used fine mesh to prevent fungal filaments from connecting seedlings to mature trees, the excluded seedlings fared worse in some cases, better in others, and no differently in most. The reviewers also found that favorable results were cited far more often than unfavorable ones, and that later papers frequently described early findings in stronger terms than the original authors had used.

None of this shows that the hypothesis is false. Carbon transfer through fungal networks may yet prove significant in particular forests or under particular conditions, and the technical obstacles to measuring it in the field are formidable. But the episode is instructive. An idea that is vivid, that flatters a wish to see cooperation in nature, and that is easy to convey to the public can acquire, through repetition, a solidity that the data never conferred on it. The appropriate response is neither to cling to the idea nor to discard it, but to design the experiments that could actually settle the matter.

rc-p2.title: Passage 2
rc-p2.markdown:
Economic historians of early modern Europe long faced a puzzle. Probate inventories, the lists of possessions drawn up when a person died, show that from the mid-seventeenth century onward ordinary households in England and the Netherlands owned a growing array of goods: clocks, mirrors, printed cottons, pottery for the newly fashionable drinks of tea and coffee. Yet estimates of daily wages for the same period show little sustained improvement. How could families whose pay was stagnant fill their homes with more things?

The historian Jan de Vries proposed an answer that he called the "industrious revolution." Households, he argued, did not earn more per day; they worked more days, and more of their members worked for money. Time once given to leisure, or to producing food and clothing for the family's own use, was redirected toward labor that earned cash, and the cash was spent on goods the market offered. On this account the change began with desire: new consumer goods tempted households to reorganize their time. The industrious revolution thus preceded the Industrial Revolution and helped prepare the ground for it, by creating both a disciplined labor force and a mass of customers before the factories arrived.

The thesis has proved fertile, but it has not gone unchallenged. Its most direct support comes from studies that reconstruct working time from indirect sources, such as the testimony of court witnesses who mentioned what they had been doing at a given hour; these suggest that the English working year lengthened considerably during the eighteenth century, in part because traditional holidays fell out of observance. Critics do not, for the most part, dispute that people worked more. They question why. If the price of bread rose faster than wages, as it did in several decades of the period, longer hours may reflect not the lure of new comforts but the pressure of old necessities. A family that sends its children to a workshop in order to eat is industrious in a sense quite different from the one de Vries intended.

The disagreement is hard to resolve because the two motives leave similar traces in the records. A longer working year looks the same in a court deposition whether it was chosen or compelled. The inventories, moreover, describe chiefly those who had property worth listing, and so may tell us least about the poorest households, for whom compulsion is most plausible. It may be that both accounts are correct for different strata of society, in which case the phrase "industrious revolution" names not one phenomenon but two.

rc-p3.title: Passage 3
rc-p3.markdown: When Emily Dickinson's poems first appeared in print in 1890, four years after her death, her editors smoothed them considerably: unconventional dashes became commas and periods, approximate rhymes were made exact, and titles were supplied for poems that had none. Not until 1955 did a scholarly edition restore the texts as they stand in her manuscripts. It has since become customary to treat the early editors as vandals who mistook originality for error. That verdict is too simple. The 1890 volume went through numerous printings within a few years, and it is doubtful that verse so strange to contemporary ears would have found those readers unaltered; the editors arguably secured the audience that made later restoration worth undertaking. None of this vindicates their changes as readings of the poems. Dickinson's dashes are not ornamental: they suspend a thought, hold alternatives open, and refuse the closure that a period imposes. To replace them is to resolve what the poet left deliberately unresolved. The editors were, in short, poor interpreters but effective advocates, and the reputation they are now accused of distorting is one they helped to create.

rc-p4.title: Passage 4
rc-p4.markdown: In the textbook model of a competitive labor market, a minimum wage set above the prevailing wage must reduce employment: firms, able to hire all the workers they want at the market rate, will hire fewer when that rate is forced upward. The prediction changes, however, if employers possess what economists call monopsony power, the ability to set wages rather than merely accept them, as may happen where a few firms dominate local hiring or where workers find it costly to change jobs. Such an employer holds wages down by hiring fewer workers than it otherwise would, since attracting an additional worker means raising pay for everyone already employed. A legal minimum removes that incentive. Up to a point, the firm required to pay more will also choose to hire more. The qualification matters: a minimum set high enough will reduce employment under either model. The dispute between the models, then, is not over whether minimum wages can destroy jobs but over how high they can rise before they begin to do so, and that is a question that theory alone cannot answer.

rc-p5.title: Passage 5
rc-p5.markdown: Why zebras are striped has been debated since the nineteenth century. The proposal most familiar to nonspecialists, that stripes camouflage the animal in tall grass or confuse predators by blurring the outlines of a fleeing herd, has fared poorly under scrutiny: at the distances from which lions typically begin a hunt, especially in dim light, their eyes probably cannot resolve the stripes at all, and zebras figure among lions' kills at least as often as their abundance would predict. A second proposal, that alternating dark and light bands set up air currents that cool the skin, has received mixed support at best. The hypothesis now best supported is at first hearing the least plausible: that stripes deter biting flies. Across the horse family, striping is most pronounced where such flies are most troublesome, and in field trials flies approached striped and unstriped coats equally often but landed on the striped ones far less. What the stripes do to an insect's vision in its final moments of approach remains unclear.

rc-p6.title: Passage 6
rc-p6.markdown: In 1973 the sociologist Mark Granovetter advanced a claim that seemed to defy common sense: in finding a job, a person's casual acquaintances are often more useful than close friends. His reasoning was structural rather than psychological. Close friends tend to know one another and to move in the same circles, so the information they hold is largely information one already has. An acquaintance, by contrast, is a bridge to circles one does not frequent, and it is across such bridges that news of an unfamiliar opening is likely to travel. Granovetter never claimed that acquaintances are more willing to help; friends are surely more motivated. His point was that motivation is useless without novel information to convey. For decades the thesis rested mainly on surveys and was difficult to test directly. A recent large-scale experiment on a professional networking site, which varied the contacts suggested to millions of users, lent it support with a refinement: the ties most likely to lead to a new job were neither the strongest nor the very weakest, but those of moderate weakness.

rc-p7.title: Passage 7
rc-p7.markdown: Few historical arguments have been as seductive as the one Lynn White Jr. published in 1962 concerning the stirrup. The device, White argued, allowed a rider to remain seated while delivering a blow with the combined weight of man and horse; this made heavily armed cavalry decisive in battle; and because such cavalry was ruinously expensive, eighth-century Frankish rulers granted land to warriors in return for mounted service, thereby laying the foundations of feudalism. A modest piece of equipment thus appeared to explain a social order. Specialists were soon unconvinced. Archaeological finds indicate that stirrups were still uncommon among the Franks at the time the land grants were supposedly made in response to them, and depictions of riders charging with the lance braced under the arm, the technique the stirrup was said to make possible, do not become common until some three centuries later. The thesis survives chiefly as a cautionary example of technological determinism: the assumption that a tool, once available, dictates the uses to which a society will put it.

rc-p8.title: Passage 8 (critical reasoning)
rc-p8.markdown: A regional bookstore chain introduced a free loyalty program that gives members a small discount on every purchase. Over the following year, members spent on average 40 percent more per visit than nonmembers did. The chain's managers concluded that membership in the program leads customers to spend more, and they plan to promote enrollment aggressively in order to raise sales.

rc-p9.title: Passage 9 (critical reasoning)
rc-p9.markdown: Two years ago a city replaced the dim orange streetlights in its central districts with much brighter white lamps. In surveys conducted since, residents of those districts say that they feel considerably safer walking at night. **Yet the number of nighttime street crimes reported to the police in those districts has not fallen; in several it has risen slightly.** City officials nonetheless maintain that the new lighting has made the streets safer than they were.

rc-p10.title: Passage 10 (critical reasoning)
rc-p10.markdown: Excavations at an ancient inland settlement have recovered pottery jars bearing residues of a fish sauce that, at the time, was produced only in a coastal region some 800 kilometers away. The jars themselves, several dozen of which were found in storerooms across the settlement, are of a type made exclusively in that region. Archaeologists have concluded that the settlement's inhabitants maintained direct trading relations with the coastal producers.

Cubing only triples each exponent. It adds no new primes. If x = 12 = 2^2 * 3, then x^3 = 2^6 * 3^3. Both have the primes 2 and 3.
Fastest method: plug in x = 2 and x = 12. Both give equal quantities, and the reasoning shows it is always so.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 2
questions.stem: When the positive integer n is divided by 7, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when 3n + 5 is divided by 7?
questions.explanation:
Plug in the easiest n, which is n = 4. Then 3n + 5 = 17, and 17 = 7*2 + 3. The remainder is 3. Check with n = 11: 38 = 7*5 + 3. Same.
The trap: answering 17 mod nothing, or choosing 4 because the remainder "stays the same".
Answer: C.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 3
questions.stem: What is the units digit of 3^47 + 4^22?
questions.explanation:
Powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1. 47 = 4*11 + 3, so 3^47 ends in 7. Powers of 4 end in 6 for even exponents, so 4^22 ends in 6. 7 + 6 = 13, so the units digit is 3.
The trap: using the remainder 3 as the answer digit instead of as a position in the cycle.
Answer: B.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 4
questions.stem: The positive integer n is divisible by both 6 and 10. Which of the following must n be divisible by?
questions.explanation:
n must be divisible by LCM(6, 10) = 30. So n is divisible by every factor of 30, including 15 and 30. Test the smallest case n = 30: it is not divisible by 12, 20 or 60.
The trap: multiplying 6 * 10 = 60 and choosing 60.
Answer: B and D.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 5
questions.stem: One light flashes every 12 seconds and another flashes every 18 seconds. They flash together at time 0. Counting the flash at time 0, how many times do they flash together during the first 10 minutes?
questions.explanation:
They flash together every LCM(12, 18) = 36 seconds. 10 minutes = 600 seconds. 600/36 = 16.67, so there are 16 joint flashes after time 0 (the last at 576 seconds). Add the one at time 0: 17.
The trap: forgetting the flash at time 0 (answering 16), or using 12 * 18 = 216.
Answer: 17.

xy < 0 means x and y have opposite signs and neither is 0. With opposite signs, the two numbers partly cancel inside |x + y|. Try x = 5, y = -3: A = 2, B = 8. Try x = -1, y = 1: A = 0, B = 2. B is always greater.
The trap: choosing C from the rule |a + b| = |a| + |b|, which is true only for same signs, or choosing D without using the condition xy < 0.
Answer: B.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 7
questions.stem: How many positive odd factors does 360 have?
questions.explanation:
360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5. An odd factor uses no 2s. So count the factors of 3^2 * 5: (2+1)(1+1) = 6. They are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45.
The trap: 24 is the total number of factors. Halving it to 12 is also wrong.
Answer: B.

questions.label: Arithmetic · Example 8
questions.stem: How many integers n satisfy |n - 4| <= 6.5?
questions.explanation:
The distance from n to 4 is at most 6.5, so -2.5 <= n <= 10.5. The integers are -2, -1, ..., 10. Count: 10 - (-2) + 1 = 13.
The trap: forgetting the "+ 1" when counting inclusive lists, or forgetting 0 and the negatives.
Answer: 13.

3. Triangle AOB has OA = OB = 6 and a 60 degree angle between them, so it is equilateral with side 6. Area = 36 * sqrt(3) / 4 = 9 * sqrt(3).

questions.stem: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
questions.explanation: 2k + 3k + 4k = 180, so k = 20. The largest angle is 4k = 80.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 3
questions.stem: A right triangle has legs of length 9 and 12. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: 9-12-15 is 3 times the 3-4-5 triple, so the hypotenuse is 15. Perimeter = 9 + 12 + 15 = 36.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 4
questions.stem: The circumference of a circle is 10 * pi.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: 2 * pi * r = 10 * pi gives r = 5. Area = 25 * pi, about 78.5. That is less than 80.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 5
questions.stem: Each interior angle of a regular polygon measures 150 degrees. How many sides does the polygon have?
questions.explanation: Each exterior angle = 180 - 150 = 30. Number of sides = 360 / 30 = 12.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 6
questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is twice its width, and its diagonal is 5 * sqrt(5). What is the area of the rectangle?
questions.explanation: Width w, length 2w. w^2 + 4w^2 = (5 * sqrt(5))^2 = 125, so w^2 = 25 and w = 5. Area = 5 * 10 = 50.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 7
questions.stem: One angle of an isosceles triangle measures 50 degrees.
questions.qa: The measure of the largest angle of the triangle, in degrees

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: If 50 is a base angle, the angles are 50, 50, 80 and the largest is 80 (equal). If 50 is the top angle, the angles are 50, 65, 65 and the largest is 65 (B greater). Two outcomes.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 8
questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle have lengths 7 and 12. Which of the following could be the length of the third side? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 12 - 7 < third side < 12 + 7, so 5 < third side < 19. The values 6, 12 and 18 work. 5 and 19 fail because the inequality is strict.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 9
questions.stem: The volume of a cube is 64. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: Edge = cube root of 64 = 4. Surface area = 6 * 16 = 96.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 10
questions.stem: The diagonal of a square has length 10.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Side = 10 / sqrt(2) = 5 * sqrt(2), about 7.07. Perimeter = 20 * sqrt(2), about 28.28, which is more than 28. Calculator-free check: 28.28^2 = 800 and 28^2 = 784.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 11
questions.stem: A circle has centre O and radius 12. Points A and B are on the circle and minor arc AB has length 4 * pi. What is the area of sector AOB?
questions.explanation: Circumference = 24 * pi. The arc is 4 * pi / (24 * pi) = 1/6 of the circle. Sector = (1/6) * pi * 144 = 24 * pi.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 12
questions.stem: In triangle PQR, angle P measures 59 degrees and angle Q measures 61 degrees.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Angle R = 180 - 59 - 61 = 60. Side PQ is opposite angle R (60). Side QR is opposite angle P (59). The bigger angle faces the longer side, so PQ > QR.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 13
questions.stem:
In trapezoid ABCD, side AB is parallel to side DC. AB = 8, DC = 20, and the two non-parallel sides are equal: AD = BC = 10. What is the area of the trapezoid?

```
        A--------B            AB = 8
       /          \
      /            \          AD = BC = 10
     D--------------C         DC = 20
```
questions.explanation: Drop perpendiculars from A and B to DC. The leftover pieces of DC on each side are (20 - 8) / 2 = 6. Each forms a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and leg 6, so the height is 8. Area = (1/2) * (8 + 20) * 8 = 112.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 14
questions.stem: The area of an equilateral triangle is 36 * sqrt(3). What is the perimeter of the triangle?
questions.explanation: s^2 * sqrt(3) / 4 = 36 * sqrt(3) gives s^2 = 144 and s = 12. Perimeter = 36.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 15
questions.stem: A rectangular box has a volume of 36, and the length of each edge is a positive integer. Which of the following could be the total surface area of the box? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: List the integer boxes with volume 36 and find 2 * (lw + lh + wh): 1 by 1 by 36 gives 146. 1 by 2 by 18 gives 112. 1 by 3 by 12 gives 102. 1 by 4 by 9 gives 98. 1 by 6 by 6 gives 96. 2 by 2 by 9 gives 80. 2 by 3 by 6 gives 72. 3 by 3 by 4 gives 66. So 66, 72, 96 and 146 are possible. 84 and 100 are not.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 16
questions.stem: A chord of length 10 is drawn in a circle of radius r.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: The longest chord is the diameter, so 10 <= 2r and r >= 5. If the chord is a diameter, r = 5 (equal). Otherwise r > 5 (A greater). Two outcomes.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 17
questions.stem: AB is a diameter of a circle and AB = 10. Point C is on the circle and is different from A and B. Which of the following could be the area of triangle ABC? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Take AB = 10 as the base. The height is the distance from C to AB, which is at most the radius, 5. So the area is at most (1/2) * 10 * 5 = 25, and it can be any positive value up to 25. 26 and 30 are too big.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 18
questions.stem: Each side of a rhombus has length 5, and one of its diagonals has length 6.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and bisect each other. Half of the known diagonal is 3. With side 5, half of the other diagonal is sqrt(25 - 9) = 4, so the other diagonal is 8. Area = 6 * 8 / 2 = 24. Equal.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 19
questions.stem: In right triangle ABC, the right angle is at C, AC = 6 and BC = 8. Point D is on AB such that CD is perpendicular to AB. What is the length of CD?
questions.explanation: AB = 10 (6-8-10). Compute the area two ways: (1/2) * 6 * 8 = 24 and (1/2) * 10 * CD = 24. So CD = 4.8.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 20
questions.stem: A cylindrical tank with radius 6 stands upright and is partly filled with water. A solid metal cube with edge 6 is lowered into the tank until it is completely under water. No water spills. By how much does the water level rise?
questions.explanation: Volume of the cube = 216. Base area of the tank = pi * 36. Rise = 216 / (36 * pi) = 6 / pi.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 21
questions.stem: A rectangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 5, so that all four vertices of the rectangle lie on the circle.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: The diagonal of the rectangle is a diameter, 10. With sides a and b: a^2 + b^2 = 100. The perimeter is largest for the square: a = b = 5 * sqrt(2), perimeter = 20 * sqrt(2), about 28.3. Proof: (a + b)^2 = 100 + 2ab, and 2ab <= a^2 + b^2 = 100, so a + b <= sqrt(200). Every such rectangle has perimeter at most 28.3, which is less than 29.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 22
questions.stem: The sides of a triangle have lengths 8, 15 and x. For which of the following values of x is the triangle obtuse (one angle greater than 90 degrees)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: First, 7 < x < 23 for a triangle. If x is the longest side: obtuse when x^2 > 64 + 225 = 289, so x > 17. That gives 18 and 22. If 15 is the longest side: obtuse when 225 > 64 + x^2, so x^2 < 161 and x <= 12. That gives 9 and 12. Check the others: x = 13 gives 64 + 169 = 233 > 225, acute. x = 17 gives a right triangle (8-15-17).

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 23
questions.stem: A circle is inscribed in a right triangle whose legs have lengths 8 and 15. The circle touches all three sides of the triangle. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse = 17 (8-15-17). r = (a + b - c) / 2 = (8 + 15 - 17) / 2 = 3. Check with r = area / half-perimeter = 60 / 20 = 3.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 24
questions.stem: A circle has centre O and radius 5. Point P is outside the circle and OP = 13. The two lines through P that are tangent to the circle touch it at points A and B. What is the length of chord AB?
questions.explanation: Radius OA is perpendicular to tangent PA, so triangle OAP is right with OA = 5, OP = 13 and PA = 12. Chord AB is perpendicular to OP, and half of AB is the height of triangle OAP from A to OP. Area two ways: (1/2) * 5 * 12 = (1/2) * 13 * h, so h = 60 / 13. AB = 2h = 120 / 13. The trap is (A), which is only half the chord.

questions.label: Geometry · Practice 25
questions.stem: Two circles each have radius 6. The centre of each circle lies on the other circle. What is the area of the region that is inside both circles?
questions.explanation: Let the centres be P and Q and let the circles cross at X and Y. PQ = PX = QX = 6, so triangle PQX is equilateral and angle XPY = 120 degrees. In each circle, the overlap contains a segment cut off by chord XY: sector (120 / 360) * pi * 36 = 12 * pi minus triangle PXY = (1/2) * 6 * 6 * sin(120) = 9 * sqrt(3). The overlap is two such segments: 2 * (12 * pi - 9 * sqrt(3)) = 24 * pi - 18 * sqrt(3), about 44.2. If you do not know sin(120): triangle PXY has base XY = 6 * sqrt(3) and height 3, area 9 * sqrt(3).

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 1
questions.stem: What is the distance between the points (-2, 3) and (4, -5)?
questions.explanation:
1. Horizontal gap: 4 - (-2) = 6. Vertical gap: -5 - 3 = -8, so 8.
2. Distance = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10.
3. Answer: C.

Fastest method: spot the 6-8-10 triple and skip the square root.

The trap: adding the gaps (14) or forgetting the square root (100).

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 2
questions.stem: Line k passes through the points (1, 2) and (3, 8).

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation:
1. Slope = (8 - 2) / (3 - 1) = 3.
2. y = 3x + b. Use (1, 2): 2 = 3 + b, so b = -1.
3. Answer: C.

Fastest method: walk back along the line. From (1, 2), go left 1 and down 3 to reach (0, -1).

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 3
questions.stem: Line p is perpendicular to the line 2x + 3y = 12 and passes through the point (4, 1). What is the x-intercept of line p?
questions.explanation:
1. 2x + 3y = 12 becomes y = -(2/3)x + 4. Its slope is -2/3.
2. The perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: 3/2.
3. Line p: y - 1 = (3/2) * (x - 4).
4. Set y = 0: -1 = (3/2) * (x - 4), so x - 4 = -2/3 and x = 10/3.
5. Answer: C.

The trap: giving the y-intercept of p, which is -5 (choice A). Read which intercept is asked.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 4
questions.stem: In the xy-plane, what is the area of the triangle bounded by the x-axis, the y-axis and the line 3x + 4y = 24?
questions.explanation:
1. x-intercept: y = 0 gives x = 8. y-intercept: x = 0 gives y = 6.
2. The triangle has vertices (0, 0), (8, 0), (0, 6). It is a right triangle with legs 8 and 6.
3. Area = (1/2) * 8 * 6 = 24.
4. Answer: 24.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 5
questions.stem: The graph of y = x^2 - 4x - 5 is drawn in the xy-plane. Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The graph crosses the x-axis at x = 5.
The vertex of the graph is (2, -9).
The graph crosses the y-axis at (0, 5).
The least value of y on the graph is -9.
The graph is symmetric about the line x = -2.

questions.explanation:
1. Factor: y = (x - 5) * (x + 1). The roots are 5 and -1. A is true.
2. The vertex is halfway between the roots: x = 2. y = 4 - 8 - 5 = -9. B is true.
3. At x = 0, y = -5, not 5. C is false.
4. a = 1 > 0, so the parabola opens upward and the vertex is the lowest point. D is true.
5. The line of symmetry is x = 2, not x = -2. E is false.
6. Answer: A, B, D.

The trap: sign slips. The y-intercept is c with its sign, and the vertex is at -b / (2a) = 4 / 2 = +2.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 6
questions.stem: In the xy-plane, the point (3, k) lies on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 25.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation:
1. 9 + k^2 = 25, so k^2 = 16.
2. k = 4 or k = -4.
3. If k = 4 the quantities are equal. If k = -4, B is greater.
4. Answer: D.

The trap: taking only the positive square root.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 7
questions.stem: The graph of y = (x - 3)^2 + 2 is shifted 5 units to the left and 4 units down. Which of the following is an equation of the new graph?
questions.explanation:
1. The fastest method is to move the vertex. The old vertex is (3, 2).
2. 5 left and 4 down: new vertex (3 - 5, 2 - 4) = (-2, -2).
3. Vertex form with vertex (-2, -2): y = (x + 2)^2 - 2.
4. Answer: A.

The trap: "left 5" means x + 5 inside the bracket, which feels backwards. Moving the vertex avoids the issue.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Example 8
questions.stem: In the xy-plane, what is the area of the region of all points (x, y) such that y >= |x| and y <= 4?
questions.explanation:
1. y >= |x| is the region on or above the V with its corner at (0, 0).
2. y <= 4 cuts it off with a horizontal line.
3. The V meets y = 4 where |x| = 4, at (-4, 4) and (4, 4).
4. The region is a triangle with vertices (0, 0), (-4, 4), (4, 4). Base 8 (along y = 4), height 4.
5. Area = (1/2) * 8 * 4 = 16. Answer: B.

```
   (-4,4) ________ (4,4)
          \      /
           \    /
            \  /
           (0,0)
```

The trap: using 4 as the base instead of 8, which gives 8.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 1
questions.stem: What is the midpoint of the segment that joins (-3, 7) and (5, -1)?
questions.explanation: Average the coordinates: x = (-3 + 5) / 2 = 1, y = (7 + (-1)) / 2 = 3.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 2
questions.stem: Line k passes through the points (0, 4) and (2, 0).

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Slope = (0 - 4) / (2 - 0) = -2. Since -2 < -1, Quantity B is greater.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 3
questions.stem: Which quadrant contains no points of the line y = 2x + 3?

options.text: The line passes through all four quadrants.

questions.explanation: Slope and y-intercept are both positive. The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 3) and the x-axis at (-1.5, 0). It rises through III, II and I. For a point in Quadrant IV you need x > 0 and y < 0, but x > 0 gives y > 3.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 5
questions.stem: A is the point (1, 1) and B is the point (4, 5).
questions.qa: The distance between A and B

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Gaps are 3 and 4. Distance = 5 (3-4-5 triple). Equal.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 6
questions.stem: Which of the following is an equation of the line that is parallel to y = -(1/2)x + 3 and passes through the point (4, 5)?
questions.explanation: Parallel means slope -1/2. y - 5 = -(1/2) * (x - 4), so y = -(1/2)x + 7. Choices C, D and E also pass through (4, 5) but have the wrong slope. Choice A has the right slope but misses the point.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 7
questions.stem: The point (a, b) lies in Quadrant II.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: a is negative and b is positive. For (-1, 3), a + b = 2 > 0. For (-3, 1), a + b = -2 < 0. Two outcomes.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 8
questions.stem: Which of the following points lie on the line 2x - 3y = 6? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Plug in: (0, -2) gives 0 + 6 = 6, yes. (3, 0) gives 6, yes. (6, 3) gives 12 - 9 = 3, no. (-3, -4) gives -6 + 12 = 6, yes. (1, -1) gives 2 + 3 = 5, no.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 9
questions.stem: At which point do the lines y = 2x + 1 and y = -x + 7 intersect?
questions.explanation: 2x + 1 = -x + 7 gives 3x = 6, x = 2, y = 5. Or back-solve: only (2, 5) fits both equations.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 10
questions.stem: Point P is (5, 2). Point Q is the reflection of P across the line y = x.
questions.qa: The distance between P and Q

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Reflection across y = x swaps the coordinates: Q = (2, 5). Distance = sqrt(9 + 9) = 3 * sqrt(2), about 4.24, which is greater than 4.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 11
questions.stem: What is the vertex of the parabola y = x^2 - 6x + 5?
questions.explanation: x = -b / (2a) = 6 / 2 = 3. y = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4. Or factor: (x - 1) * (x - 5), roots 1 and 5, vertex at x = 3.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 12
questions.stem: The line y = mx + b passes through Quadrants I, II and IV, and does not pass through Quadrant III.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: To pass through II and I and then go down into IV while missing III, the line must cross the y-axis above the origin (b > 0) and fall to the right (m < 0). So m * b is negative.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 13
questions.stem: Which of the following points lie inside the circle x^2 + y^2 = 100 (not on it)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Compute x^2 + y^2 and compare with 100. (6, 8): 100, on the circle. (7, 7): 98, inside. (-8, 5.5): 64 + 30.25 = 94.25, inside. (0, -10): 100, on the circle. (9, 5): 106, outside. (-1, 9.9): 1 + 98.01 = 99.01, inside.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 14
questions.stem: What is the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (7, 1) and (4, 6)?
questions.explanation: The side from (1, 1) to (7, 1) is horizontal with length 6. The height is the vertical distance from (4, 6) to the line y = 1, which is 5. Area = (1/2) * 6 * 5 = 15.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 15
questions.stem: Which of the following lines are perpendicular to the line 4x - 2y = 7? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: 4x - 2y = 7 gives y = 2x - 3.5, slope 2. Perpendicular slope is -1/2. Slopes of the choices: A is -1/2. B is -1/2. C is -2. D is 1/2. E is -3/6 = -1/2.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 16
questions.stem: Line L passes through the point (2, 3) and has a negative slope.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: With slope m < 0: x-intercept = 2 - 3/m and y-intercept = 3 - 2m. If m = -1, both are 5 (equal). If m = -3, the x-intercept is 3 and the y-intercept is 9 (B greater). If m = -1/2, they are 8 and 4 (A greater).

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 17
questions.stem: The line through (2, 3) and (6, k) is perpendicular to the line through (0, 0) and (3, 6). What is the value of k?
questions.explanation: The second line has slope 6 / 3 = 2, so the first has slope -1/2. (k - 3) / (6 - 2) = -1/2 gives k - 3 = -2, k = 1. Choice E (11) comes from making the lines parallel.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 18
questions.stem: The graph of y = |x - 2| - 3 crosses the x-axis at two points.
questions.qa: The distance between the two points

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: Set y = 0: |x - 2| = 3, so x = 5 or x = -1. The distance is 6. Equal.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 19
questions.stem: What is the area of the quadrilateral with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (8, 4) and (2, 4), taken in that order?
questions.explanation: The sides from (0, 0) to (6, 0) and from (2, 4) to (8, 4) are both horizontal with length 6, so the shape is a parallelogram with base 6 and height 4. Area = 24.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 20
questions.stem: The line y = x + 4 intersects the circle x^2 + y^2 = 10 at points A and B. What is the length of AB?
questions.explanation: Substitute y = x + 4: x^2 + (x + 4)^2 = 10, so 2x^2 + 8x + 6 = 0, x^2 + 4x + 3 = 0, x = -1 or x = -3. Points (-1, 3) and (-3, 1). Distance = sqrt(4 + 4) = 2 * sqrt(2).

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 21
questions.stem: a > b > 0. Line 1 has equation y = ax + 5 and Line 2 has equation y = bx + 5.

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation: x-intercepts: -5/a and -5/b. Since a > b > 0, 5/a < 5/b, so -5/a > -5/b. Example: a = 5, b = 1 gives -1 and -5, and -1 is greater. The steeper line reaches the x-axis sooner, closer to the origin.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 22
questions.stem: The line y = 2x + k intersects the parabola y = x^2 at two different points. Which of the following could be the value of k? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Set x^2 = 2x + k: x^2 - 2x - k = 0. Two different solutions need the discriminant 4 + 4k > 0, so k > -1. The values -1/2, 0 and 4 work. k = -1 gives exactly one point (the line is tangent). k = -3 gives none.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 23
questions.stem: What is the area of the triangle bounded by the three lines y = 2x, y = x/2 and y = -x + 6?
questions.explanation: Find the corners. y = 2x and y = x/2 meet at (0, 0). y = 2x and y = -x + 6: 3x = 6, point (2, 4). y = x/2 and y = -x + 6: 1.5x = 6, point (4, 2). With one vertex at the origin, area = |ad - bc| / 2 = |2 * 2 - 4 * 4| / 2 = 12 / 2 = 6.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 24
questions.stem: The parabola y = a * (x - 1) * (x - 5) has a highest point, and the y-coordinate of that point is 8. What is the y-intercept of the parabola?
questions.explanation: The roots are 1 and 5, so the vertex is at x = 3. There y = a * (2) * (-2) = -4a = 8, so a = -2. At x = 0: y = -2 * (-1) * (-5) = -10.

questions.label: Coordinate Geometry · Practice 25
questions.stem: A circle has its centre at (3, 4) and passes through the origin. Which of the following is an equation of the line that is tangent to the circle at the origin?
questions.explanation: The radius to the origin runs from (3, 4) to (0, 0) and has slope 4/3. The tangent is perpendicular to it, so its slope is -3/4. It passes through the origin, so y = -(3/4)x. Choice E has the right slope but does not pass through the origin.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 1
questions.stem: The average (arithmetic mean) of 5 numbers is 12. When one of the numbers is removed, the average of the remaining 4 numbers is 10. What number was removed?
questions.explanation:
1. Sum of the 5 numbers = 5 * 12 = 60.
2. Sum of the remaining 4 = 4 * 10 = 40.
3. Removed number = 60 - 40 = 20. Answer: D.

The trap: thinking the answer is 12 + 2 = 14. Removing one value moved the average of FOUR numbers by 2, so the removed value is 12 + 4 * 2 = 20.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 2

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation:
1. Sum = 40, so the mean is 8.
2. The list is sorted. The middle (third) value is 7.
3. 8 > 7. Answer: A.

Fastest method: the high value 14 sits further from the middle than the low value 3, so it drags the mean above the median.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 3
questions.stem: In a class, 20 students took a test in the morning and their average score was 70. The other 30 students took it in the afternoon and their average score was 80. What was the average score for all 50 students?
questions.explanation:
1. Morning total = 20 * 70 = 1,400. Afternoon total = 30 * 80 = 2,400.
2. Combined total = 3,800.
3. Average = 3,800 / 50 = 76. Answer: 76.

The trap: answering 75, the plain average of 70 and 80. The afternoon group is bigger, so the answer is closer to 80.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 4
questions.qa: The standard deviation of list P
questions.qb: The standard deviation of list Q

options.text: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.explanation:
1. Both lists have mean 5.
2. In P, three values sit exactly on the mean and two are 4 away.
3. In Q, only one value sits on the mean and four are 4 away.
4. Q is more spread out around the mean. Answer: B.

The trap: saying "equal" because both lists have the same mean and the same range. Do not compute. Compare distances from the mean.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 5
questions.stem: The scores on a test are approximately normally distributed with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100. Approximately what percent of the scores are between 400 and 700?
questions.explanation:
1. 400 is 1 SD below the mean. 700 is 2 SDs above the mean.
2. From 400 to 500: 34 percent.
3. From 500 to 700: 34 + 13.5 = 47.5 percent.
4. Total = 81.5 percent. Answer: B.

The trap: the interval is not symmetric, so neither 68 nor 95 applies. Split at the mean and add the two sides.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 6
questions.stem: The median of the five numbers 4, 8, 9, 12 and x is 9. Which of the following could be the value of x? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
1. Without x the sorted list is 4, 8, 9, 12. With five numbers the median is the third.
2. If x >= 9, the sorted list starts 4, 8, 9 and the third value is 9. This works.
3. If x <= 8, the third value becomes 8. Test x = 8: 4, 8, 8, 9, 12 has median 8. This fails.
4. Answer: C, D, E.

questions.label: Statistics · Example 8

The table shows the number of errors found on each of 20 pages.

|---|---|
| 0 | 2 |
| 1 | 5 |
| 2 | 8 |
| 3 | 4 |
| 4 | 1 |

By how much does the median number of errors exceed the mean number of errors?
questions.explanation:
1. Mean: total errors = 0 * 2 + 1 * 5 + 2 * 8 + 3 * 4 + 4 * 1 = 37. Mean = 37 / 20 = 1.85.
2. Median: with 20 values it is the average of the 10th and 11th. Count up: pages with 0 errors are positions 1 to 2, pages with 1 error are positions 3 to 7, pages with 2 errors are positions 8 to 15. Both the 10th and 11th are 2.
3. Median - mean = 2 - 1.85 = 0.15. Answer: B.

The trap: averaging the left column (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) or the right column and ignoring the frequencies.

questions.qb: The standard deviation of five consecutive integers

Case x >= 8: the median is 8, so 37 + x = 56 and x = 19. That fits. Case x = 6 or 7: the median is x, so 37 + x = 7x and x = 37/6, not an integer. So x is -2 or 19. Three different integers below 20 are needed, so a1 is at most 17, with a2 = 18 and a3 = 19. Then a7 = 32, and the best a5 and a6 are 30 and 31. Sum = 17 + 18 + 19 + 20 + 30 + 31 + 32 = 167. Choice A (113) is the least possible sum.

questions.label: Counting and Probability · Example 1
questions.stem: How many odd 3-digit positive integers have three different digits?
questions.explanation:
1. Use slots and fill the most restricted first.
2. Units digit must be odd: 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. That is 5 options.
3. Hundreds digit cannot be 0 and cannot equal the units digit: 8 options.
4. Tens digit can be anything except the two digits used: 8 options.
5. 5 * 8 * 8 = 320. Answer: B.

The trap: filling the hundreds digit first with 9 options. Then the count for the units digit depends on whether the hundreds digit was odd, and the simple product (C) is wrong.

questions.label: Counting and Probability · Example 2
questions.stem: A committee of 3 people is to be chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many different committees include at least one woman?
questions.explanation:
1. Order does not matter, so use combinations.
2. All committees: C(9, 3) = (9 * 8 * 7) / 6 = 84.
3. Committees with no women (all men): C(5, 3) = 10.
4. At least one woman = 84 - 10 = 74. Answer: 74.

The trap: "pick one woman, then any 2 of the remaining 8": 4 * C(8, 2) = 112. This counts committees with two or three women more than once.

questions.label: Counting and Probability · Example 3
questions.stem: How many different arrangements of the six letters in the word LETTER are there?
questions.explanation:

2. Arrangements = 6! / (2! * 2!) = 720 / 4 = 180. Answer: C.

The trap: 6! = 720 treats the two E's (and the two T's) as different letters.

questions.stem: Five people, including Ana and Ben, are to stand in a row for a photo. In how many of the possible orders are Ana and Ben NOT next to each other?

2. Orders with Ana and Ben together: glue them into one block. 4 blocks can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways, and inside the block there are 2 orders. 24 * 2 = 48.
3. Not together = 120 - 48 = 72. Answer: D.

The trap: stopping at 48, or forgetting the factor of 2 inside the block.

questions.label: Counting and Probability · Example 6
questions.stem: A bag contains 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that the two marbles are the same colour?
questions.explanation:
1. Same colour means both red OR both blue. These cases do not overlap, so add.
2. Both red: (5/8) * (4/7) = 20/56.
3. Both blue: (3/8) * (2/7) = 6/56.
4. Total = 26/56 = 13/28. Answer: C.

Check with combinations: (C(5, 2) + C(3, 2)) / C(8, 2) = (10 + 3) / 28.

The trap: (E) is the answer with replacement. (B) is only the red case. (D) is the probability of different colours.

questions.label: Counting and Probability · Example 7
questions.stem: For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Which of the following could be the value of P(A or B)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation:
1. P(A or B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - P(A and B) = 0.9 - P(A and B).
2. The overlap P(A and B) is at least 0 (mutually exclusive) and at most 0.4 (B lies completely inside A).
3. So P(A or B) is between 0.9 - 0.4 = 0.5 and 0.9 - 0 = 0.9, and any value in between is possible. For example, if A and B are independent, the overlap is 0.2 and P(A or B) = 0.7.
4. Answer: B, C, D.

The trap: assuming the events are independent or mutually exclusive when the question does not say so.

2. Sequences with exactly 2 heads: C(4, 2) = 6.
3. Probability = 6/16 = 3/8, which is less than 1/2.

The trap: "half heads is the most likely result, so the probability is 1/2". It is the most likely count, but it still happens less than half the time.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 6
questions.stem: The theory's elegance has made it (i) _____ among physicists, yet elegance is no guarantee of truth: several of its central predictions remain (ii) _____ by experiment.
questions.explanation: **B, D (popular; unsupported).** Clues: "elegance has made it _____ ... yet elegance is no guarantee of truth". Elegance attracts, so the first blank is positive; the colon then gives the reason for doubt: predictions lack experimental backing. Trap: *suspect* fits the doubtful mood of the second half but leaves "yet" with nothing to contrast. Vocab: *suspect* (adjective) = doubtful, not to be trusted.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 7
questions.stem: Unlike her predecessor, whose (i) _____ pronouncements left investors guessing about the bank's intentions, the new governor has been (ii) _____ about the conditions under which interest rates will rise.
questions.explanation: **A, E (cryptic; explicit).** Clues: "Unlike her predecessor" requires opposites; "left investors guessing" defines the first blank as hard to interpret. Trap: *evasive* matches the predecessor, not the new governor. Vocab: *cryptic* = mysterious, hard to interpret; *forthright* = direct and open.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 8
questions.stem: The apparent (i) _____ of the desert is deceptive; beneath the surface, dormant seeds and burrowing animals wait for the brief rains that will transform the landscape into one of startling (ii) _____.
questions.explanation: **A, E (sterility; profusion).** Clues: "apparent ... is deceptive" means the desert only looks lifeless; the semicolon explains that life is waiting ("dormant seeds", "burrowing animals") and the rains "transform" it. The second blank is the opposite of lifelessness: abundance. Trap: *aridity* (dryness) is true of deserts but cannot be what rain produces. Vocab: *profusion* = great abundance.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 9
questions.stem: Though the memoir purports to be a (i) _____ record of the expedition, the author's habit of omitting episodes that reflect poorly on him gives it the character of (ii) _____.
questions.explanation: **B, D (faithful; an apologia).** Clues: "purports to be" signals a claim that is not fully true; "omitting episodes that reflect poorly on him" shows the book really defends its author. Trap: *a chronicle* is a neutral record, which is what the book pretends to be, not what it actually is. Vocab: *purports* = claims; *apologia* = a formal defense of one's own conduct; *elegy* = a poem or text of mourning.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 10
questions.stem: The notion that language determines thought has had a (i) _____ history. Embraced enthusiastically in the mid-twentieth century, it was later (ii) _____ as experimental support failed to materialize; more recently, a (iii) _____ version, holding that language merely influences certain habits of perception, has regained respectability.
questions.explanation: **A, E, H (checkered; discredited; tempered).** Clues: the story has ups and downs: "embraced enthusiastically", then "support failed to materialize", then a version that says language "merely influences" has "regained respectability". Trap: *radical* for blank (iii) contradicts "merely influences", which is a weaker claim. Vocab: *checkered* = marked by alternating good and bad periods; *vindicated* = proved right; *tempered* = moderated.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 11
questions.stem: Urban planners often assume that widening a congested road will (i) _____ traffic. Studies of induced demand suggest the opposite: added capacity (ii) _____ additional drivers, so that within a few years congestion is frequently as (iii) _____ as before.
questions.explanation: **A, E, H (alleviate; entices; severe).** Clues: planners expect widening to help. "Suggest the opposite" plus "so that ... congestion is ... as _____ as before" means new capacity pulls in new drivers and congestion returns. Trap: *deters* is the opposite direction: if capacity deterred drivers, congestion would fall. Vocab: *alleviate* = make less severe; *induced demand* = extra use created by extra supply.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set B · 12
questions.stem: The painter's late canvases, once dismissed as the (i) _____ efforts of a failing talent, are now seen as deliberately spare. What earlier critics took for (ii) _____ was in fact (iii) _____: every omitted detail was a considered choice.
questions.explanation: **A, E, G (feeble; incapacity; economy).** Clues: "once dismissed as ... efforts of a failing talent" needs a negative word; "now seen as deliberately spare" and "every omitted detail was a considered choice" show the sparseness was skill. So critics took it for inability, and it was in fact economy of means. Trap: *restraint* for (ii) leaves no contrast with (iii): restraint and economy are both deliberate virtues. Vocab: *economy* (in art) = using only what is needed.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 1
questions.stem: The diplomat's memoir is a model of _____: it manages to describe three decades of negotiations without once committing its author to a judgment that any party could find objectionable.
questions.explanation: **A (circumspection).** Clues: the colon defines the blank: "without once committing its author to a judgment that any party could find objectionable". That is extreme caution about what one says. Trap: *candor* (frankness) is what memoirs are usually praised for, but this one avoids frank judgments altogether. Vocab: *circumspection* = wary caution; *erudition* = deep learning; *concision* = brevity.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 2
questions.stem: That the study's authors were funded by the very industry whose product they evaluated does not, in itself, _____ their conclusions, though it does oblige readers to scrutinize the methodology with particular care.
questions.explanation: **B (vitiate).** Clues: "does not, in itself, _____ their conclusions, though it does oblige readers to scrutinize". The funding is a reason for suspicion, but the sentence says it does not go as far as invalidating the results. Trap: *corroborate* (confirm) reverses the logic: no one would think industry funding confirms a study. Vocab: *vitiate* = spoil or invalidate; *elucidate* = make clear; *presage* = foreshadow; *recapitulate* = summarize.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 3
questions.stem: The essayist's prose, often praised as limpid, is in fact merely _____: its surface simplicity conceals not depth but an absence of anything requiring complex expression.
questions.explanation: **B (facile).** Clues: "often praised as limpid, is in fact merely _____" asks for a negative version of clear and simple; the colon specifies: simplicity with nothing underneath. Trap: *lapidary* (polished and concise) is a prose-style word, but it is praise, and "merely" needs a fault. *Turgid* and *abstruse* contradict "surface simplicity". Vocab: *limpid* = clear; *facile* = superficially easy, shallow; *turgid* = swollen, pompous; *abstruse* = hard to understand; *mordant* = bitingly sarcastic.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 4
questions.stem: Scholars who treat the treaty as a triumph of statesmanship overlook how much it owed to _____: neither signatory wanted the agreement so much as each lacked the means to continue the war.
questions.explanation: **C (exhaustion).** Clues: "overlook how much it owed to _____" contrasts with "triumph of statesmanship", and the colon explains: each side "lacked the means to continue the war". The peace came from being worn out, not from wisdom. Trap: *foresight* and *magnanimity* are statesmanlike virtues, exactly what the sentence denies. Vocab: *magnanimity* = generosity toward a rival; *duplicity* = deceit; *intransigence* = refusal to compromise.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 5
questions.stem: The architect's reputation for _____ is not wholly deserved: although his public buildings are indeed austere, the private houses he designed abound in ornament and playful detail.
questions.explanation: **A (severity).** Clues: "not wholly deserved: although his public buildings are indeed austere". "Indeed" confirms that the reputation is for austerity; the private houses "abound in ornament and playful detail", which is the exception. Trap: *whimsy* describes the private houses, not the reputation. Vocab: *severity* (of style) = plainness, strictness; *eclecticism* = drawing on many styles; *probity* = moral integrity.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 6
questions.stem: The reviewer's objection is not that the biography is (i) _____, for its scholarship is impeccable, but that its author, in her determination to be fair to every faction, has produced a portrait so (ii) _____ that the subject's notoriously abrasive personality never comes into focus.
questions.explanation: **A, D (inaccurate; anodyne).** Clues: "not that the biography is _____, for its scholarship is impeccable" means the first blank is a fault that impeccable scholarship excludes. The second: trying "to be fair to every faction" produced a portrait in which an "abrasive personality never comes into focus", so it is bland. Trap: *tendentious* (biased) is the opposite of being fair to every faction. Vocab: *anodyne* = inoffensive to the point of blandness; *impeccable* = faultless.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 7
questions.stem: Proponents of the reform describe its costs as (i) _____, but this characterization is (ii) _____: the expenditures will recur annually and are projected to grow.
questions.explanation: **B, D (transitory; disingenuous).** Clues: after the colon, the costs "will recur annually and are projected to grow". That refutes a claim that the costs are temporary, and a claim made by "proponents" that conflicts with known facts is not candid. Trap: *unavoidable* sounds like something proponents would say, but recurring costs do not show that a cost is avoidable. Vocab: *transitory* = temporary; *disingenuous* = not sincere, pretending to know less than one does; *prohibitive* = too high to pay.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 8
questions.stem: In science, a hypothesis that accommodates every conceivable observation is not thereby (i) _____; on the contrary, its very (ii) _____ deprives it of explanatory power, since a claim that forbids nothing asserts nothing.
questions.explanation: **A, D (strengthened; elasticity).** Clues: "is not thereby _____; on the contrary" plus "deprives it of explanatory power" means fitting everything looks like a strength but is a weakness. "Its very _____" names the property of stretching to fit any observation. Trap: *precision* is a scientific virtue, but a claim "that forbids nothing" is the opposite of precise. Vocab: *elasticity* = ability to stretch.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 9
questions.stem: The poet's early admirers mistook (i) _____ for profundity; only when the difficulties of her syntax had been patiently worked through did it become apparent how (ii) _____ the underlying thoughts were.
questions.explanation: **A, D (obscurity; commonplace).** Clues: "mistook _____ for profundity" means the poems seemed deep only because they were hard ("difficulties of her syntax"). Once worked through, the thoughts turn out to be ordinary. Trap: *intricate* or *subversive* would make the thoughts genuinely impressive, which contradicts "mistook". Vocab: *commonplace* = ordinary, unoriginal; *lucidity* = clarity.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 10
questions.stem: It would be a mistake to regard the guild system as simply (i) _____ to innovation. Guilds did restrict entry into trades, but they also (ii) _____ technical knowledge through apprenticeship, and the standards they enforced gave distant buyers a reason to (iii) _____ goods they could not inspect themselves.
questions.explanation: **A, E, G (inimical; transmitted; trust).** Clues: "It would be a mistake to regard ... as simply _____" followed by "did restrict ... but they also" means the common view is negative and the sentence adds positives: passing on knowledge "through apprenticeship" and giving buyers confidence in goods "they could not inspect". Trap: *hoarded* fits the negative stereotype of guilds but cannot follow "but they also". Vocab: *inimical* = hostile, harmful; *conducive* = helpful to.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 11
questions.stem: The physicist was (i) _____ popularizer: she held that any idea that could not be explained to a curious twelve-year-old had not been fully understood by the explainer. Colleagues who (ii) _____ such work as a distraction from research were, in her view, confusing (iii) _____ with rigor.
questions.explanation: **B, E, G (an unapologetic; disparaged; opacity).** Clues: the colon shows she believed firmly in explaining simply, so she popularized without embarrassment. Colleagues who saw it "as a distraction" looked down on it, and she thought they confused being hard to understand with being rigorous. Trap: *a reluctant* popularizer is a familiar phrase, but her stated principle shows conviction, not reluctance. Vocab: *disparaged* = belittled; *opacity* = lack of clarity.

questions.label: Text Completion · Set C · 12
questions.stem: Economic historians have grown (i) _____ of accounts that attribute industrialization to a single cause. The availability of coal, for instance, was surely (ii) _____, yet regions equally rich in coal failed to industrialize for another century, which suggests that coal alone was hardly (iii) _____.
questions.explanation: **B, E, G (chary; significant; sufficient).** Clues: historians distrust single-cause accounts. "Surely _____, yet" concedes that coal mattered; "regions equally rich in coal failed to industrialize" shows that having coal was not enough by itself. Trap: *necessary* for (iii): the evidence (coal without industry) tests sufficiency, not necessity. Vocab: *chary* = cautious, wary; *enamored* = fond; *heedless* = careless of.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 1
questions.stem: Although the subject itself is fascinating, the professor's delivery was so _____ that several students struggled to stay awake.
questions.explanation: **A, C (tedious, monotonous).** Clues: "Although the subject ... is fascinating" sets up a contrast, and "so _____ that ... struggled to stay awake" gives the result. Trap: *animated* and *lively* are a perfect synonym pair in the wrong direction. Vocab: *erudite* = learned (it would not put students to sleep by itself).

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 2
questions.stem: The company's profits had been climbing steadily for years, but they _____ once a cheaper competitor entered the market.
questions.explanation: **A, D (plummeted, plunged).** Clues: "had been climbing ... but" requires a reversal, and a cheaper competitor explains a sharp fall. Trap: *soared* and *surged* are synonyms that continue the climb, ignoring "but". *Stabilized* fits the sentence alone (climbing, then flat) but has no partner. Vocab: *fluctuated* = moved up and down.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 3
questions.stem: Known for her _____, the judge listened to both sides patiently and never let personal feelings influence her rulings.
questions.explanation: **A, C (impartiality, fairness).** Clues: "listened to both sides" and "never let personal feelings influence her rulings". Trap: *severity* and *harshness* are a synonym pair associated with judges, but nothing in the sentence is about strict punishment.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 4
questions.stem: The instructions were so _____ that even experienced technicians could not agree on what they meant.
questions.explanation: **A, C (ambiguous, unclear).** Clues: "so _____ that even experienced technicians could not agree on what they meant". Trap: *detailed* and *thorough* form a pair, but thorough instructions would produce agreement, not confusion. Vocab: *concise* = brief and clear.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 5
questions.stem: The once-thriving port is now _____, its warehouses empty and its docks rotting.
questions.explanation: **B, E (derelict, dilapidated).** Clues: "once-thriving ... now" signals decline; "warehouses empty and docks rotting" describes a place fallen into ruin. Trap: *bustling* and *thriving* are synonyms that describe the past, not the present. Vocab: *derelict* = abandoned and in ruins; *dilapidated* = fallen into disrepair; *picturesque* = charming to look at.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 6
questions.stem: Critics praised the debut novel for its _____ prose, which conveyed complex emotions in remarkably few words.
questions.explanation: **B, D (economical, spare).** Clues: "in remarkably few words". Trap: *verbose* and *wordy* are a pair with the opposite meaning. *Lyrical* is a natural compliment for prose and fits alone, but it says nothing about few words and has no partner. Vocab: *spare* = plain, without excess; *ornate* = heavily decorated.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 7
questions.stem: The treaty brought only a _____ peace; within two years the two nations were at war again.
questions.explanation: **B, D (transient, short-lived).** Clues: "only a _____ peace" and the semicolon explanation: "within two years ... at war again". Trap: *lasting* and *durable* are a pair in the opposite direction. *Hard-won* is a common phrase with "peace" but clashes with "only" and has no partner. Vocab: *transient* = lasting a short time.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 8
questions.stem: Far from being _____, the new manager turned out to be one of the most approachable people in the office.
questions.explanation: **A, C (aloof, distant).** Clues: "Far from being _____ ... one of the most approachable people". The blank is the opposite of approachable. Trap: *affable* and *friendly* are synonyms of "approachable", so they destroy the contrast. Vocab: *aloof* = cool and remote; *affable* = pleasant, easy to talk to.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 9
questions.stem: The scientist was _____ about the early results, warning that they had not yet been replicated.
questions.explanation: **A, C (cautious, guarded).** Clues: "warning that they had not yet been replicated". Trap: *jubilant* and *elated* (both = overjoyed) are a pair that contradicts the warning. *Secretive* looks close to *guarded*, but she is speaking openly, just carefully.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 10
questions.stem: Because the evidence against the defendant was entirely _____, the jury was reluctant to convict.
questions.explanation: **A, C (circumstantial, indirect).** Clues: "Because ... the jury was reluctant to convict" means the evidence was weak in kind. Trap: *conclusive* and *irrefutable* are synonyms that would make a jury eager to convict. Vocab: *circumstantial* = suggesting a fact without proving it directly; *forensic* = relating to scientific methods of investigating crime.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 11
questions.stem: The committee's decision to postpone the vote yet again was widely seen as an attempt to _____ the issue rather than confront it.
questions.explanation: **A, C (evade, sidestep).** Clues: "rather than confront it" requires the opposite of confronting; postponing "yet again" is avoidance. Trap: *resolve* and *settle* are a pair, but postponing a vote does not settle anything. *Study* fits alone loosely and has no partner.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set A · 12
questions.stem: Her _____ remarks at the funeral, delivered with a grin, struck many mourners as inappropriate.
questions.explanation: **A, D (flippant, frivolous).** Clues: "delivered with a grin" and "inappropriate" at a funeral: the remarks lacked seriousness. Trap: *somber* and *solemn* are a pair that suits funerals, so they would not strike anyone as inappropriate. Vocab: *flippant* = not showing proper seriousness.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 1
questions.stem: The author's latest book is a _____ of her earlier work: the same arguments reappear, supported by the same examples.
questions.explanation: **B, D (rehash, restatement).** Clues: the colon explains: "the same arguments reappear, supported by the same examples". Trap: *repudiation* and *refutation* are near-synonyms meaning rejection, which is the opposite of repeating. *Refinement* is tempting, but refining implies improvement and the sentence stresses sameness. Vocab: *rehash* = old material presented again with little change; *repudiation* = rejection; *vindication* = proof of being right.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 2
questions.stem: Even the most _____ supporters of the policy concede that its implementation has been badly flawed.
questions.explanation: **A, C (ardent, fervent).** Clues: "Even the most _____ supporters ... concede". "Even" needs the extreme case: the strongest supporters. Trap: *lukewarm* and *tepid* are a perfect synonym pair, but weak supporters conceding a flaw is not surprising, so "even" makes no sense. Vocab: *ardent*, *fervent* = passionate; *tepid* = half-hearted.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 3
questions.stem: The chief executive's _____ response to the scandal, a single sentence released late on a Friday, did little to reassure shareholders.
questions.explanation: **A, C (terse, laconic).** Clues: "a single sentence". Trap: *effusive* and *gushing* are a pair meaning overflowing with words or feeling, the opposite. *Belated* is tempting because of "late on a Friday", but that describes the timing in the week, not lateness of the response, and it has no partner. Vocab: *terse*, *laconic* = using few words; *contrite* = sincerely sorry.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 4
questions.stem: Although the two theories are often presented as _____, a careful reading shows that each can accommodate the other's central claims.
questions.explanation: **B, D (irreconcilable, incompatible).** Clues: "Although ... often presented as _____, ... each can accommodate the other's central claims". The common presentation is the opposite of "can accommodate". Trap: *compatible* and *complementary* agree with the second clause, leaving "although" with no contrast. Vocab: *irreconcilable* = impossible to bring into agreement; *obsolete* = out of date.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 5
questions.stem: Long _____ by its mountain setting, the village preserved features of dialect that had vanished elsewhere centuries earlier.
questions.explanation: **A, C (isolated, secluded).** Clues: the village "preserved" old dialect features that "vanished elsewhere", which is what happens when a place is cut off from outside contact. Trap: *imperiled* and *endangered* are synonyms, but being in danger does not explain preservation. *Impoverished* fits a mountain village alone, but has no partner and no link to dialect. Vocab: *secluded* = shut off from others; *imperiled* = put in danger.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 6
questions.stem: The reviewer found the film's ending _____: after two hours of careful buildup, the plot was resolved by a coincidence that no viewer could have accepted.
questions.explanation: **A, C (contrived, artificial).** Clues: the colon explains: resolved "by a coincidence that no viewer could have accepted". Trap: *poignant* and *moving* are a pair that praises the ending, but the sentence criticizes it. *Abrupt* could describe such an ending but has no partner, and the complaint is implausibility, not speed. Vocab: *contrived* = obviously forced, not natural; *poignant* = touching.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 7
questions.stem: The senator's opponents accused her of _____, pointing out that she had privately promised her vote to both sides.
questions.explanation: **A, C (duplicity, deceitfulness).** Clues: "privately promised her vote to both sides" is double-dealing. Trap: *naivety* and *credulity* are a pair, but they describe someone easily fooled, not someone fooling others. *Indecision* is tempting, but making two secret promises is deception, not hesitation. Vocab: *duplicity* = deliberate deceit, double-dealing; *credulity* = readiness to believe anything.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 8
questions.stem: What the documentary presents as a _____ discovery was in fact the culmination of decades of deliberate, incremental research.
questions.explanation: **A, C (serendipitous, fortuitous).** Clues: "What the documentary presents as ... was in fact ... decades of deliberate, incremental research". The blank is the opposite of deliberate: a lucky accident. Trap: *painstaking* and *laborious* are a pair that agrees with "deliberate", so "in fact" would have nothing to correct. *Momentous* fits alone and has no partner. Vocab: *serendipitous*, *fortuitous* = happening by lucky chance.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 9
questions.stem: The new regulations, intended to simplify the licensing process, have instead made it more _____.
questions.explanation: **B, D (convoluted, byzantine).** Clues: "intended to simplify ... have instead". The result is the opposite of simple. Trap: *streamlined* and *efficient* are a pair that matches the intention, not the outcome. Vocab: *convoluted* = extremely complicated; *byzantine* = excessively intricate and hard to navigate.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 10
questions.stem: The professor was known for her _____ standards: she returned any paper containing even a single unsupported claim.
questions.explanation: **A, C (exacting, stringent).** Clues: the colon: she returned any paper with "even a single unsupported claim". Trap: *lax* and *lenient* are a pair with the opposite meaning. *Arbitrary* is wrong because her rule is consistent and has a reason. Vocab: *exacting* = demanding great care; *stringent* = strict.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 11
questions.stem: Despite its _____ beginnings in a rented garage, the firm now employs more than ten thousand people.
questions.explanation: **A, C (humble, modest).** Clues: "Despite ... beginnings in a rented garage ... now employs more than ten thousand". The beginnings were small. Trap: *auspicious* and *promising* are a pair, but "despite promising beginnings" would need a disappointing outcome. Vocab: *auspicious* = suggesting future success.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set B · 12
questions.stem: The curator's catalog essay is admirably _____: it assumes no prior knowledge and explains each technical term as it arises.
questions.explanation: **A, C (accessible, approachable).** Clues: "assumes no prior knowledge and explains each technical term". Trap: *recondite* and *esoteric* are a pair meaning understood only by specialists, the opposite. *Scholarly* and *comprehensive* each sound right for a catalog essay, but neither is what the colon explains, and neither has a partner. Vocab: *recondite* = obscure, little known; *esoteric* = meant for a small group with special knowledge.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 1
questions.stem: The minister's apology was widely regarded as _____: it acknowledged that mistakes had been made without specifying what they were or who had made them.
questions.explanation: **A, E (evasive, equivocal).** Clues: the colon: it "acknowledged that mistakes had been made without specifying what they were or who had made them". The apology avoids committing to anything. Trap: *heartfelt* and *sincere* are a pair in the wrong direction. *Abject* (utterly humble) is a common partner of "apology" but the wrong meaning. *Grudging* is negative and tempting, but the fault described is vagueness, not unwillingness, and it has no partner. Vocab: *equivocal* = deliberately vague or ambiguous.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 2
questions.stem: The philosopher's argument, though ingenious, is ultimately _____: it appears to prove its conclusion only because that conclusion has been smuggled into the premises.
questions.explanation: **A, E (specious, fallacious).** Clues: "though ingenious, is ultimately _____" needs a fault; it "appears to prove" its conclusion only by assuming it. An argument that looks sound but is not. Trap: *cogent* and *compelling* are a pair of praise words that ignore "though". *Abstruse* (hard to follow) is a fault, but not the one described. Vocab: *specious* = seeming true but actually false; *fallacious* = based on faulty reasoning; *cogent* = convincing; *prolix* = too wordy.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 3
questions.stem: Having expected the veteran negotiator to be _____, the delegates were disconcerted by her readiness to concede point after point.
questions.explanation: **A, C (intransigent, obdurate).** Clues: "Having expected ... were disconcerted by her readiness to concede". The expectation was the opposite of conceding: stubbornness. Trap: *pliant* and *tractable* are a pair meaning easily persuaded, which is what she turned out to be, not what was expected. Vocab: *intransigent* = refusing to compromise; *obdurate* = stubbornly unyielding; *tractable* = easy to manage; *urbane* = polished and courteous.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 4
questions.stem: The biographer resists the temptation to _____ her subject, recording his pettiness and vanity as scrupulously as his achievements.
questions.explanation: **A, C (exalt, glorify).** Clues: she "resists the temptation" and records "pettiness and vanity as scrupulously as his achievements". The temptation is to show only the good side. Trap: *disparage* and *denigrate* are a pair, but a biographer tempted to belittle would not be resisting by recording faults. *Scrutinize* fits "scrupulously" by association, yet she does scrutinize him, so it is not something she resists. Vocab: *denigrate* = unfairly criticize; *emulate* = imitate.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 5
questions.stem: The treatise is _____ to a fault: no assertion, however minor, is allowed to pass without a paragraph of qualification and a page of footnotes.
questions.explanation: **A, C (punctilious, scrupulous).** Clues: "to a fault" means a virtue carried too far, and the colon shows which virtue: no claim passes without qualification and footnotes, which is extreme care about accuracy. Trap: *slipshod* and *slapdash* are a pair meaning careless, the opposite. *Prolix* (wordy) fits the result quite well, but "to a fault" requires a quality that is normally good, and it has no partner. Vocab: *punctilious* = attentive to every detail of correctness; *derivative* = unoriginal.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 6
questions.stem: Reports of the technology's demise have proved _____; a decade after analysts wrote it off, it still underlies most of the world's financial transactions.
questions.explanation: **A, D (premature, precipitate).** Clues: the semicolon: a decade after it was "written off", it "still underlies" most transactions. The reports came too soon. Trap: *prescient* and *prophetic* are a pair meaning correctly foreseeing, the opposite of what happened. Vocab: *precipitate* (adjective) = hasty, done too soon; *demise* = death, end.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 7
questions.stem: The council's new guidelines are so _____ that officials on opposite sides of the dispute have each cited them in support of their positions.
questions.explanation: **A, D (nebulous, indeterminate).** Clues: "so _____ that officials on opposite sides ... have each cited them". Guidelines that support both sides are vague. Trap: two synonym pairs here. *Explicit* and *unequivocal* (clear) are the opposite; *draconian* and *stringent* (harsh, strict) are about severity, which does not explain both sides claiming support. Vocab: *nebulous* = vague, cloudy; *draconian* = excessively harsh.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 8
questions.stem: The novelist's reputation for misanthropy is hard to square with her letters, which reveal a _____ and unfailingly generous correspondent.
questions.explanation: **A, D (genial, cordial).** Clues: "hard to square with" a reputation for misanthropy, plus "and unfailingly generous": the blank is a warm, friendly quality. Trap: *caustic* and *acerbic* are a pair that matches the reputation, not the letters. *Prolific* suits a correspondent but does not contradict misanthropy and has no partner. Vocab: *misanthropy* = dislike of people; *caustic*, *acerbic* = sharply sarcastic.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 9
questions.stem: Skeptics regard the firm's sudden enthusiasm for environmental causes as _____, noting that it coincided exactly with the announcement of a government inquiry into its emissions.
questions.explanation: **A, C (opportunistic, self-serving).** Clues: "Skeptics" and the timing: it "coincided exactly with" an inquiry into the firm's emissions. They think the enthusiasm serves the firm's interests. Trap: *altruistic* and *disinterested* are a pair (disinterested means unbiased, having no personal stake, not bored), and they are the opposite of what skeptics think. *Belated* fits alone but has no partner. Vocab: *quixotic* = idealistic and impractical.
