questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 10
questions.stem: The study's conclusions, while suggestive, rest on evidence too _____ to justify the sweeping policy changes its authors recommend.
questions.explanation: **A, C (tenuous, slender).** Clues: "while suggestive" concedes a little; "too _____ to justify the sweeping policy changes" needs "weak, thin". Trap: *substantial* and *copious* are a pair meaning plentiful, the opposite. *Recent* could fit alone (evidence too new) but has no partner. Vocab: *tenuous* = thin, weak; *copious* = abundant.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 11
questions.stem: Although he affected an air of _____, those who worked closely with the director knew how anxiously he monitored every review.
questions.explanation: **A, C (insouciance, nonchalance).** Clues: "Although he affected an air of _____" contrasts with "how anxiously he monitored every review". He pretended not to care. Trap: *diligence* and *assiduity* are a pair, but hard work is consistent with anxious monitoring, so there is no contrast. Vocab: *affected* = pretended to have; *insouciance*, *nonchalance* = casual lack of concern; *assiduity* = persistent hard work.

questions.label: Sentence Equivalence · Set C · 12
questions.stem: The historian's claim that the reform was inevitable is _____ by her own evidence, which shows how narrowly the measure passed and how easily it might have failed.
questions.explanation: **A, C (belied, undercut).** Clues: the claim is "inevitable"; her own evidence shows "how narrowly the measure passed and how easily it might have failed". The evidence contradicts the claim. Trap: *buttressed* and *bolstered* are a pair meaning supported, the opposite direction. *Complicated* fits alone, but it is weaker than the two answers and has no partner. Vocab: *belied* = shown to be false; *buttressed* = supported.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 1 · Q1
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: describe how mycorrhizal fungi obtain nutrients from the trees they colonize
argue that a widely accepted claim about fungal networks goes beyond the evidence that supports it
demonstrate that trees do not transfer carbon to one another
propose a new experimental technique for tracing the movement of carbon in forests
criticize journalists for misrepresenting ecological research to the public

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: the passage accepts that networks exist ("not in dispute"), then examines the sharing claim and finds the evidence "far thinner than its reputation suggests", ending with a lesson about ideas that gain "a solidity that the data never conferred". Tempting wrong answer: C is too strong. The last paragraph says "None of this shows that the hypothesis is false." E is wrong because the passage blames repetition and citation habits among researchers as well, and journalists are never named.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 1 · Q2
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

According to the passage, which of the following is a reason to doubt that the isotope experiment demonstrated ecologically significant transfer of carbon through fungal networks?

options.text: The labeled carbon could have reached the neighboring tree by way of the soil.
The amounts of labeled carbon detected were generally small compared with what seedlings produce for themselves.
Carbon located in the fungal tissue around a seedling's roots may not be available to the seedling.

questions.explanation: **A, B and C (all three).** Proof for A: "Labeled carbon can move through the soil itself ... without any fungal intermediary." Proof for B: "the quantities detected were in most cases small relative to what a seedling fixes through its own photosynthesis." Proof for C: "carbon found in the fungal tissue sheathing a seedling's roots is not necessarily carbon that the seedling itself can use." Trap: many students assume a select-all question never has all three correct. It can.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 1 · Q3
questions.stem: Select the sentence in the third paragraph that describes a pattern in how researchers reported or referred to earlier findings, as distinct from a pattern in the experimental results themselves.
questions.answer: The reviewers also found that favorable results were cited far more often than unfavorable ones
questions.explanation: **"The reviewers also found that favorable results were cited far more often than unfavorable ones ..."** Proof: this sentence is about citation and description by later papers. Tempting wrong answer: the mesh sentence ("In experiments that used fine mesh ...") describes a pattern in the results themselves, which the question excludes.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 1 · Q4
questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the hypothesis that trees share ecologically significant resources through fungal networks is best described as

options.text: convinced that it is false and ought to be abandoned
persuaded that it is true but has been poorly communicated
doubtful that existing evidence supports it, yet open to its being confirmed
indifferent, on the grounds that the question can never be settled
confident that future experiments will vindicate it

questions.explanation: **C.** Proof: doubt is shown by "far thinner than its reputation suggests"; openness is shown by "None of this shows that the hypothesis is false" and "may yet prove significant", and by the call for decisive experiments. Tempting wrong answer: A ignores "neither to cling to the idea nor to discard it". E is too optimistic: "may yet prove" is a possibility, not a prediction.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 2 · Q5
questions.stem: The first paragraph of the passage serves primarily to

options.text: summarize a thesis that the remainder of the passage refutes
present an apparent inconsistency in the evidence that the thesis introduced in the next paragraph attempts to resolve
call into question the reliability of probate inventories as historical sources
describe the consumer habits that caused the Industrial Revolution
contrast economic conditions in England with those in the Netherlands

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: the paragraph sets growing possessions against flat wages and ends with a question ("How could families whose pay was stagnant fill their homes with more things?"). The second paragraph begins "proposed an answer". Tempting wrong answer: A, because the first paragraph states a puzzle, not a thesis, and the rest of the passage qualifies de Vries without refuting him.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 2 · Q6
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

Based on the passage, the critics mentioned in the third paragraph would be likely to accept which of the following statements?

options.text: English workers in the eighteenth century came to work more days per year than their predecessors had.
Households lengthened their working time chiefly because they wanted newly available consumer goods.
For at least part of the period, the cost of basic food rose more quickly than pay.

questions.explanation: **A and C.** Proof for A: "Critics do not, for the most part, dispute that people worked more." Proof for C: the critics' argument rests on bread prices that rose faster than wages, "as it did in several decades of the period". B is wrong: it is de Vries's own explanation, and it is exactly what the critics question ("They question why").

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 2 · Q7
questions.stem: In the context in which it appears, "fertile" (first sentence of the third paragraph) most nearly means
questions.explanation: **B (productive).** Proof: "The thesis has proved fertile, but it has not gone unchallenged", followed by a description of the studies and debate it generated. A fertile thesis is one that produces further work. Tempting wrong answer: A (inventive) describes a creative mind, not what a thesis gives rise to. D (persuasive) is contradicted by "not gone unchallenged". Vocab: *lush* = growing thickly, the literal sense of fertile land.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 2 · Q8
questions.stem: The passage suggests that probate inventories are of limited use in resolving the disagreement because they

options.text: were drawn up only after death and so cannot show when goods were acquired
give the least information about the households whose motives are most in question
exaggerate the quantity of goods that ordinary households owned
record only goods that were produced outside the home
survive in large numbers for England but not for the Netherlands

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: "The inventories ... describe chiefly those who had property worth listing, and so may tell us least about the poorest households, for whom compulsion is most plausible." Tempting wrong answer: A is a reasonable real-world criticism of inventories, but the passage never makes it. Stay inside the text.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 3 · Q9
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?

options.text: Dickinson's early editors deserve more blame than they have received for altering her poems.
The 1955 edition of Dickinson's poems is superior in every respect to the edition of 1890.
Although the early editors' alterations misrepresented the poems, those editors helped win the readership on which Dickinson's reputation rests.
Dickinson's unconventional punctuation was the chief reason her poems were not published during her lifetime.
Nineteenth-century readers were incapable of appreciating original poetry.

questions.explanation: **C.** Proof: the last sentence summarizes the whole passage: "poor interpreters but effective advocates, and the reputation they are now accused of distorting is one they helped to create." Tempting wrong answer: A takes only the critical half and reverses the author's "That verdict is too simple". B is too absolute ("in every respect") and is not the point.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 3 · Q10
questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author reports a commonly held view that the passage goes on to qualify.
questions.answer: It has since become customary to treat the early editors as vandals who mistook originality for error.
questions.explanation: **"It has since become customary to treat the early editors as vandals who mistook originality for error."** Proof: "customary" marks a common view, and the next sentence qualifies it: "That verdict is too simple." Tempting wrong answer: "That verdict is too simple" is the author's own judgment, not the reported view.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 3 · Q11
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

The passage suggests which of the following about Dickinson's dashes?

options.text: They contribute to the meaning of the poems in which they appear.
They were introduced into the poems by the scholarly edition of 1955.
They leave open possibilities that conventional punctuation would close off.

questions.explanation: **A and C.** Proof for A: "Dickinson's dashes are not ornamental." Proof for C: "they suspend a thought, hold alternatives open, and refuse the closure that a period imposes." B is wrong: the 1955 edition "restore[d] the texts as they stand in her manuscripts", so the dashes were Dickinson's own. The trap in B is the word "introduced".

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 3 · Q12
questions.stem: The author mentions the number of printings of the 1890 volume primarily in order to

options.text: show that the early editors profited financially from their alterations
support the suggestion that the altered poems quickly reached a substantial audience
prove that readers who saw the manuscript versions of the poems rejected them
explain why the restoration of the texts was delayed until 1955
indicate that Dickinson's poems had been widely read during her lifetime

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: the printings are followed directly by "it is doubtful that verse so strange ... would have found those readers unaltered; the editors arguably secured the audience". The figure shows the edited book found many readers quickly. Tempting wrong answer: C. Readers in 1890 never saw the manuscript versions, and the author says only that it is "doubtful", not proven.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 4 · Q13
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: argue that minimum wage laws generally increase employment
show that the predicted effect of a minimum wage on employment depends on how much power employers have over wages and on how high the minimum is set
refute the textbook model of a competitive labor market
explain why workers find it costly to change jobs
recommend a specific level at which the minimum wage should be set

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: the passage gives the competitive prediction, shows that "The prediction changes" under monopsony, then adds that "a minimum set high enough will reduce employment under either model". Tempting wrong answer: A. The passage says a minimum can raise employment only "Up to a point" and only where employers have wage-setting power. C is wrong because the textbook model is limited, not refuted.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 4 · Q14
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

According to the passage, an employer with monopsony power

options.text: is able to influence the wage it pays instead of simply taking the market wage as given
would respond to a moderate legal minimum wage by employing fewer workers
must be the only employer in its local labor market

questions.explanation: **A only.** Proof for A: monopsony power is defined as "the ability to set wages rather than merely accept them". B is wrong: "Up to a point, the firm required to pay more will also choose to hire more." C is wrong: monopsony "may happen where a few firms dominate local hiring or where workers find it costly to change jobs", so a single employer is not required. Trap: assuming a select-all question must have at least two correct answers.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 4 · Q15
questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage most strongly implies that

options.text: economists should abandon theoretical models of the labor market
finding the level at which a minimum wage starts to reduce employment requires evidence from actual labor markets
the two models make identical predictions about moderate minimum wages
no minimum wage has ever reduced employment
the monopsony model describes most labor markets more accurately than the competitive model does

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: "that is a question that theory alone cannot answer". If theory alone cannot, something other than theory, namely observation of real markets, is needed. Tempting wrong answer: A goes much too far; "alone" means theory is insufficient, not useless. E is unsupported: the passage never says which model is more accurate.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 4 · Q16
questions.stem: Select the sentence that explains why an employer with monopsony power restricts the number of workers it hires.
questions.answer: Such an employer holds wages down by hiring fewer workers than it otherwise would, since attracting an additional worker means raising pay for everyone already employed.
questions.explanation: **"Such an employer holds wages down by hiring fewer workers than it otherwise would, since attracting an additional worker means raising pay for everyone already employed."** Proof: the "since" clause gives the reason. Tempting wrong answer: the sentence defining monopsony power ("The prediction changes, however ...") says what the power is and when it arises, not why it leads to less hiring.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 5 · Q17
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

The passage cites which of the following as evidence against the view that stripes protect zebras from predators?

options.text: Lions probably cannot make out the stripes from the distances at which they usually start to hunt.
Zebras are not underrepresented among the animals that lions kill.
Striping in the horse family is most pronounced in regions where biting flies are a serious problem.

questions.explanation: **A and B.** Proof for A: lions' "eyes probably cannot resolve the stripes at all" at hunting distances. Proof for B: "zebras figure among lions' kills at least as often as their abundance would predict". C is a true statement from the passage, but it is offered as support for the fly hypothesis, not as evidence against the predator hypothesis. Always check what the detail is used for.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 5 · Q18
questions.stem: The results of the field trials described in the passage most strongly suggest that stripes

options.text: make an animal harder for flies to detect from a distance
interfere with flies at the stage of landing rather than at the stage of approach
repel flies by chemical rather than visual means
protect zebras from diseases that flies carry
are effective against flies only in dim light

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: "flies approached striped and unstriped coats equally often but landed on the striped ones far less", and the final sentence refers to the insect's "final moments of approach". Tempting wrong answer: A is contradicted by "approached ... equally often". C introduces chemistry, which the passage never mentions.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 5 · Q19
questions.stem: In the context in which it appears, "resolve" most nearly means
questions.explanation: **B (distinguish).** Proof: the subject is lions' eyes at a distance in dim light; for eyes to "resolve" stripes is to see them as separate bands. Tempting wrong answer: A (settle) is the most common meaning of "resolve", which is why vocabulary-in-context questions must be answered from the sentence, not from memory.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 5 · Q20
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the support that the field trials provide for the biting-fly hypothesis?

options.text: The striped coats used in the trials had been washed in a substance known to repel flies, whereas the unstriped coats had not.
Some species of biting fly transmit diseases that can be fatal to horses.
Lions do most of their hunting at night.
The pattern of stripes differs from one individual zebra to another.
Unstriped members of the horse family that live where flies are scarce tend to have thicker coats.

questions.explanation: **A.** Proof: the trials support the hypothesis only if the stripes themselves caused fewer landings. If the striped coats alone carried a fly repellent, the repellent explains the result and the stripes are not needed. Tempting wrong answer: E concerns the geographic correlation, not the field trials that the question asks about, and it does not undermine either. B, if anything, adds a reason why deterring flies would matter.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 6 · Q21
questions.stem: According to the passage, Granovetter held that casual acquaintances are valuable to a job seeker chiefly because they

options.text: are more eager to help than close friends are
greatly outnumber a person's close friends
have access to information that does not circulate among the job seeker's close friends
are trusted by employers more than close friends are
are less likely than close friends to be competing for the same position

questions.explanation: **C.** Proof: close friends hold "largely information one already has", while an acquaintance "is a bridge to circles one does not frequent". Tempting wrong answer: A is explicitly denied: "Granovetter never claimed that acquaintances are more willing to help".

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 6 · Q22
questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the author heads off a possible misunderstanding of Granovetter's claim.
questions.answer: Granovetter never claimed that acquaintances are more willing to help; friends are surely more motivated.
questions.explanation: **"Granovetter never claimed that acquaintances are more willing to help; friends are surely more motivated."** Proof: "never claimed" signals a correction of a reading someone might mistakenly adopt. Tempting wrong answer: "His reasoning was structural rather than psychological" hints at the same idea but does not name the misunderstanding.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 6 · Q23
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

Which of the following is consistent with the results of the experiment as the passage describes them?

options.text: A person's closest friends are the contacts most likely to lead that person to a new job.
Contacts with whom a person has almost no connection are less useful in finding a job than somewhat closer acquaintances.
Granovetter's thesis, though broadly supported, needed to be made more precise.

questions.explanation: **B and C.** Proof for B: the most useful ties were "neither the strongest nor the very weakest, but those of moderate weakness". Proof for C: the experiment "lent it support with a refinement". A is wrong: the strongest ties were not the most likely to lead to a job.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 6 · Q24
questions.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the reasoning attributed to Granovetter in the passage?

options.text: A nurse hears of a vacancy on her own ward from a close colleague with whom she eats lunch every day.
An accountant learns that a firm in another city is hiring from a former classmate whom he sees once every few years.
A graphic designer finds a position by answering a public advertisement.
A teacher is hired at a school because her sister, who is the principal, recommends her.
A chef turns down a job offer passed on to him by a casual acquaintance.

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: a rarely seen former classmate is a weak tie, and a firm "in another city" is an unfamiliar circle; the job news crosses a "bridge". Tempting wrong answer: D involves a contact who helps a great deal, but it shows motivation by a strong tie, the factor Granovetter set aside. A is a strong tie passing on information from the job seeker's own circle. C involves no personal tie at all.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 7 · Q25
questions.stem:
Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply.

According to the passage, which of the following counts against White's argument?

options.text: Stirrups were not yet in wide use among the Franks when the land grants were made.
The style of fighting that the stirrup was said to enable became common only long after the eighth century.
Heavily armed cavalry was much less expensive to maintain than White supposed.

questions.explanation: **A and B.** Proof for A: "stirrups were still uncommon among the Franks at the time the land grants were supposedly made". Proof for B: depictions of the braced-lance charge "do not become common until some three centuries later". C is wrong: the expense of cavalry is part of White's argument and the passage never disputes it.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 7 · Q26
questions.stem: By calling White's argument "seductive," the author most likely means that it is

options.text: appealing in its neatness and scope, though not for that reason well founded
convincingly supported by the available evidence
popular only among readers who are not specialists

questions.explanation: **B.** Proof: the passage admires the argument's reach ("A modest piece of equipment thus appeared to explain a social order") and then shows that "Specialists were soon unconvinced". Seductive here means attractive but misleading. Tempting wrong answer: A. Nothing suggests White intended to deceive; an argument can be alluring and honestly mistaken. C is contradicted by the evidence in the second half.

questions.label: Reading Comprehension · Passage 7 · Q27
questions.stem: Which of the following statements would most likely be made by a technological determinist, as that position is characterized in the passage?

options.text: "Once printing with movable type existed, the spread of literacy throughout society was bound to follow."
"Societies adopt new tools only when their existing institutions create a demand for them."
"The same invention has been put to quite different uses by different cultures."
"Military innovations tend to be costly, and so are available only to wealthy rulers."
"Archaeological evidence is more reliable than written sources."

questions.explanation: **A.** Proof: the passage defines technological determinism as "the assumption that a tool, once available, dictates the uses to which a society will put it". Statement A has exactly that form: the tool exists, so the social result "was bound to follow". Tempting wrong answer: B and C are the anti-determinist position (society decides how tools are used). D sounds like White's argument about cost but says nothing about tools dictating outcomes.

questions.label: Critical Reasoning · Passage 8 · Q28
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the managers' conclusion?

options.text: Customers who chose to enroll were, on average, already spending considerably more per visit than other customers before the program began.
Several competing chains offer loyalty programs with larger discounts.
The discount reduces the profit the chain earns on each sale to a member.
Members visited the stores more often than nonmembers did.
The chain's total sales rose slightly during the year.

questions.explanation: **A.** The managers move from a correlation (members spend more) to a cause (membership makes people spend more). A gives the alternative explanation: big spenders chose to join, so the difference existed before the program. Tempting wrong answer: C is a real business problem for the plan, but the question asks about the conclusion that membership "leads customers to spend more", and lower profit per sale does not touch that. D is about frequency of visits, not spending per visit.

questions.label: Critical Reasoning · Passage 8 · Q29
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the managers' conclusion?

options.text: In the year before the program began, the customers who later enrolled spent about the same amount per visit as those who did not.
A majority of the chain's regular customers enrolled in the program.
In a survey, members said that they liked the program.
Most nonmembers were occasional visitors from outside the region.
The chain raised its prices during the year.

questions.explanation: **A.** If future members and nonmembers spent the same per visit beforehand, the difference appeared only after enrollment, which rules out the "big spenders joined" explanation and supports a causal reading. Tempting wrong answer: D actually weakens: it gives another pre-existing difference between the groups. C shows satisfaction, not increased spending.

questions.label: Critical Reasoning · Passage 9 · Q30
questions.stem: In the argument above, the sentence in boldface plays which of the following roles?

options.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.
It is evidence that the officials offer in support of their position.
It is a finding that appears to conflict with the position the officials maintain.
It is an explanation of the survey results.
It is an assumption on which the residents' responses depend.

questions.explanation: **C.** Proof: "Yet" introduces the crime figures as a contrast to the survey results, and "nonetheless" shows that the officials hold their position in spite of them. Tempting wrong answer: B. The officials do not cite this fact; it is the obstacle to their claim. A is wrong because the passage's final sentence, not the bold one, states the position being maintained.

questions.label: Critical Reasoning · Passage 9 · Q31
questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the officials' position with the crime figures?

options.text: Under the brighter lights, victims and passersby are far more likely to see an offense clearly and report it, so a larger share of the crimes that occur are now reported.
The new lamps cost less to operate than the old ones.
Residents of districts that kept the old streetlights also say they feel safer than they did two years ago.
The number of crimes reported during daylight hours has not changed.
The surveys were conducted by the company that manufactures the new lamps.

questions.explanation: **A.** The puzzle: lighting is said to make streets safer, yet reported crime did not fall. If brighter light raises the share of crimes that get reported, the number of crimes actually committed could have fallen while the number reported stayed level or rose. Tempting wrong answer: C deepens the puzzle (people feel safer even without new lights, so the feeling may have nothing to do with the lamps). E undermines the surveys but does nothing to reconcile the crime figures with the officials' claim.

questions.label: Critical Reasoning · Passage 10 · Q32
questions.stem: The archaeologists' conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?

options.text: The jars did not reach the settlement by passing through the hands of intermediary traders.
The inhabitants of the settlement were unable to produce a fish sauce of their own.
The coastal region exported fish sauce to no other inland settlement.
Fish sauce was a luxury available only to the wealthy.
The inhabitants of the settlement paid for the jars with goods rather than with coin.

questions.explanation: **A.** The evidence shows only that the jars and sauce originated on the coast. To conclude that the settlement traded directly with the producers, the argument must assume the goods did not arrive through middlemen. Negation test: if the jars did pass through intermediary traders, the conclusion of direct trade collapses. Tempting wrong answer: B. The passage already states the sauce was produced only on the coast, and even if the settlement could make its own, the coastal jars would still need explaining. C is irrelevant: exports to other settlements do not affect whether this trade was direct.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 1
questions.stem: Though the critics ______ the director's first film as a masterpiece, they dismissed his second as a failure.
questions.explanation: A, lauded. "As a masterpiece" needs a word of praise, and "though" sets it against the later dismissal.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 2
questions.stem: The witness was so ______ that the lawyer had to drag each one-word answer out of him.
questions.explanation: D, reticent. One-word answers that must be dragged out show unwillingness to speak.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 3
questions.stem: Despite hours of pleading from both families, the landlord remained ______ and refused to delay the eviction by even a day.
questions.explanation: A, obdurate. He is unmoved by pleading, which is the core of obdurate.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 4
questions.stem: The argument seemed convincing at first, but on closer inspection it proved ______, resting on a hidden error in logic.
questions.explanation: B, specious. Specious means looking sound while actually being false.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 5
questions.stem: Fame gained through a viral video is usually ______; within a month the public has moved on.
questions.explanation: C, ephemeral. The public moves on within a month, so the fame is very short-lived.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 6
questions.stem: Rather than give a direct answer, the spokesman ______, using phrases vague enough to satisfy both sides.
questions.explanation: C, equivocated. Deliberately vague language used to avoid commitment is equivocation.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 7
questions.stem: Because clay is ______ when wet, a potter can shape it into almost any form.
questions.explanation: A, malleable. Something that can be shaped into any form is malleable.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 8
questions.stem: The editor asked for a ______ summary, no longer than three sentences, of the 200-page report.
questions.explanation: C, succinct. Three sentences for 200 pages means brief and clear.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 9
questions.stem: After a month-long strike that emptied its warehouses, the company finally ______ and accepted every one of the union's demands.
questions.explanation: C, capitulated. Accepting every demand after resisting is surrender.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 10
questions.stem: The laws of arithmetic are ______: two plus two will equal four in every country and every century.
questions.explanation: A, immutable. Something true everywhere and always cannot change.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 11
questions.stem: The senator's ______ speech ran for three hours and sent half the chamber to sleep.
questions.explanation: B and D, verbose and prolix. Both mean wordy and too long. Pithy is the opposite.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 12
questions.stem: Investors avoid the currency because its value is so ______, rising and falling sharply from one day to the next.
questions.explanation: C and D, erratic and volatile. Sharp daily rises and falls are unpredictable change.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 13
questions.stem: The reviewer ______ the novel, calling it clumsy, dull and dishonest.
questions.explanation: B and E, castigated and lambasted. Both mean to criticize harshly. Extolled and venerated are praise.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 14
questions.stem: Her ______ manner was a contrast to the scheming of her colleagues; she said exactly what she thought and hid nothing.
questions.explanation: C and D, artless and guileless. The contrast with scheming calls for words meaning without deceit.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 15
questions.stem: Negotiations failed because the union leader was ______, rejecting every compromise that was offered.
questions.explanation: D and F, obstinate and intransigent. Rejecting every compromise is stubbornness. Amenable and compliant are opposites.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 16
questions.stem: A ______ man, the lighthouse keeper could pass a whole week without speaking ten words.
questions.explanation: A and F, taciturn and laconic. Both describe someone of very few words. Voluble and loquacious are a pair with the opposite meaning.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 17
questions.stem: The children ______ the old storyteller, treating her every word as precious.
questions.explanation: C and F, revered and venerated. Treating every word as precious shows deep respect.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 18
questions.stem: The committee ______ for months between the two designs, favoring one on Monday and the other by Friday.
questions.explanation: B and F, wavered and vacillated. Switching back and forth between two choices is vacillating or wavering.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 19
questions.stem: The reasoning behind the proposal was ______: it looked sound but collapsed under the first serious question.
questions.explanation: B and D, fallacious and specious. Reasoning that looks sound but is wrong is specious or fallacious.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 20
questions.stem: The relief was ______; within an hour the pain had returned.
questions.explanation: C and E, fleeting and transient. Relief gone within an hour is short-lived. Perennial and abiding mean long-lasting.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, terse. The other four mean talkative or wordy. Terse means brief.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, extol. The other four mean to criticize or scold. Extol means to praise.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, adamant. The other four mean easy to influence or control. Adamant means refusing to be persuaded.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, acquiesce. The other four involve deceiving or hiding the truth. Acquiesce means to accept without protest.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 1 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: C, steadfast. The other four mean changeable. Steadfast means firm and unchanging.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 1
questions.stem: The new medication did little to ______ her pain; if anything, the side effects made her feel worse.
questions.explanation: C, alleviate. The drug was expected to ease the pain but did little, so the blank means to lessen.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 2
questions.stem: Far from calming the dispute, the minister's careless remark ______ it, bringing thousands more protesters onto the streets.
questions.explanation: A, exacerbated. "Far from calming" signals the opposite: the remark made things worse.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 3
questions.stem: The professor's explanation was so ______ that even first-year students understood the theory at once.
questions.explanation: D, lucid. Everyone understood at once, so the explanation was clear.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 4
questions.stem: Too ______ to speak up in meetings, the talented analyst watched others take credit for her ideas.
questions.explanation: C, diffident. She lacks the confidence to speak, which is diffidence.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 5
questions.stem: The ______ heir ran through a fortune in three years, buying yachts he never sailed.
questions.explanation: E, prodigal. Wasting a fortune on unused yachts is wasteful extravagance.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 6
questions.stem: The scientist was careful to ______ her claim, noting that the results applied only to mice and might not hold for humans.
questions.explanation: B, qualify. Adding limits to a statement is to qualify it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 7
questions.stem: With attendance low and several members absent, the council voted to ______ the motion until its next session.
questions.explanation: A, table. "Until its next session" shows the motion was postponed.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 8
questions.stem: In his ______, the champion refused to train, certain that no challenger could ever beat him.
questions.explanation: D, hubris. Certainty that nobody can beat him is excessive pride.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 9
questions.stem: Stranded for days, the sailors ______ their remaining water, allowing each man only a mouthful at dawn and dusk.
questions.explanation: B, husbanded. Rationing a mouthful at a time is using a resource sparingly.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 10
questions.stem: The contract's language was deliberately ______, so that neither party could be sure what had actually been promised.
questions.explanation: A, equivocal. Language that leaves both parties unsure is open to two readings.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 11
questions.stem: The airline offered vouchers to ______ the passengers who had been stranded overnight.
questions.explanation: B and E, placate and mollify. Vouchers are meant to calm angry passengers.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 12
questions.stem: The treatise is so ______ that only a few specialists claim to understand it.
questions.explanation: D and F, esoteric and abstruse. Understood by only a few specialists means hard to understand.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 13
questions.stem: The ______ waiter looked down his nose at anyone who ordered the cheapest wine.
questions.explanation: A and E, haughty and supercilious. Looking down on others is haughty or supercilious behavior.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 14
questions.stem: A ______ employer, he counted every paper clip and refused to replace a broken chair.
questions.explanation: A and B, miserly and parsimonious. Counting paper clips shows extreme unwillingness to spend.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 15
questions.stem: Years of illness had ______ him, leaving him too weak to climb a single flight of stairs.
questions.explanation: B and E, debilitated and enervated. "Too weak" shows he was drained of strength. Enervate means to weaken.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 16
questions.stem: The falsehood of his statement was ______ to everyone who had watched the recording.
questions.explanation: C and D, manifest and patent. Those who saw the recording could plainly see the lie, so it was obvious.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 17
questions.stem: The palace was famous for its ______ halls, hung with silk and lined with gold.
questions.explanation: C and E, opulent and lavish. Silk and gold indicate rich luxury.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 18
questions.stem: She ______ her criticism with praise for the team's effort, so that no one left the meeting discouraged.
questions.explanation: A and B, qualified and tempered. Softening criticism with praise is to temper or qualify it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 19
questions.stem: New witnesses ______ the prosecution's case, which now looked far stronger than it had a week before.
questions.explanation: C and F, bolstered and buttressed. The case looks stronger, so the witnesses strengthened it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 20
questions.stem: Her note was so ______ that we spent an hour trying to work out what she meant.
questions.explanation: C and F, cryptic and enigmatic. A note that takes an hour to interpret is puzzling.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, aggravate. The other four mean to make better or less severe. Aggravate means to make worse.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: D, meek. The other four describe pride or self-importance. Meek means gentle and submissive.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, profligate. The other four describe careful or stingy spending. Profligate means recklessly wasteful.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: C, explicit. The other four mean hard to understand. Explicit means clearly stated.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 2 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: D, pretentious. The other four describe modesty or shyness. Pretentious means trying to seem important.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 1
questions.stem: The guard gave the passports only a ______ glance, missing the fact that two of them had expired.
questions.explanation: B, cursory. A glance that misses expired passports was quick and not thorough.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 2
questions.stem: Decades of ______ between the two families ended only when their children married.
questions.explanation: D, enmity. Something lasting decades and ended by a marriage is hostility.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 3
questions.stem: The phrase was once fresh, but endless repetition in advertisements has made it ______.
questions.explanation: B, hackneyed. Overuse has removed its freshness, which is the meaning of hackneyed.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 4
questions.stem: Only a ______ buyer would believe that a genuine diamond could cost so little.
questions.explanation: D, credulous. Believing an unlikely claim shows too much readiness to believe.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 5
questions.stem: A second laboratory ______ the finding by repeating the experiment and obtaining the same result.
questions.explanation: D, corroborated. The same result from a repeat confirms the finding.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 6
questions.stem: The typewriter is now ______, having been replaced almost everywhere by the computer.
questions.explanation: E, obsolete. Something replaced almost everywhere is no longer in use.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 7
questions.stem: His cheerful tone ______ the seriousness of the news he had come to deliver.
questions.explanation: A, belied. A cheerful tone gives a false impression of serious news.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 8
questions.stem: An ______ worker, she stayed late every evening to check her figures a third time.
questions.explanation: C, assiduous. Staying late to check a third time shows persistent hard work.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 9
questions.stem: The policy is ______: it saves a little money this year but will cost a great deal more within ten.
questions.explanation: A, myopic. Short-term saving at long-term cost is short-sighted.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 10
questions.stem: With no witnesses and no documents, his version of events remained pure ______.
questions.explanation: C, conjecture. A claim with no evidence is a guess.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 11
questions.stem: It was ______ of the nurse to leave the medicine cabinet unlocked.
questions.explanation: C and E, negligent and remiss. Leaving the cabinet unlocked is a failure of proper care.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 12
questions.stem: The ______ editor checked every date, name and figure in the manuscript twice.
questions.explanation: A and F, meticulous and fastidious. Checking everything twice shows great attention to detail. Cursory and perfunctory are opposites.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 13
questions.stem: The general's ______ speech, full of threats against neighboring states, alarmed diplomats.
questions.explanation: A and F, belligerent and bellicose. Threats against neighbors are warlike and hostile.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 14
questions.stem: The lecture was a string of ______ observations that everyone in the hall had heard many times before.
questions.explanation: A and D, trite and banal. Remarks heard many times before are ordinary and overused.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 15
questions.stem: An ______ negotiator, she saw at once what the other side wanted most and used it to her advantage.
questions.explanation: B and C, shrewd and astute. Seeing and using an advantage quickly shows sharp judgment.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 16
questions.stem: Reporters were ______ about the company's claim, since it had made similar promises before and broken them.
questions.explanation: A and C, skeptical and dubious. Broken promises in the past give reason to doubt.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 17
questions.stem: The divorce was settled without ______; the couple remained on friendly terms.
questions.explanation: D and E, acrimony and rancor. Remaining friendly means there was no bitterness.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 18
questions.stem: The ______ industry, only two years old, has not yet attracted government regulation.
questions.explanation: A and D, incipient and nascent. Only two years old means just beginning. Obsolete and antiquated mean out of date.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 19
questions.stem: She has long ______ the cause of free education, speaking for it at every opportunity.
questions.explanation: C and E, espoused and advocated. Speaking for a cause at every opportunity is supporting it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 20
questions.stem: The chatter at the party was so ______ that he slipped away early to read.
questions.explanation: D and F, vapid and inane. Chatter dull enough to escape from is empty and silly.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: A, indolent. The other four describe hard, careful work. Indolent means lazy.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, consensus. The other four mean hostility or bitterness. Consensus means general agreement.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: D, novel. The other four mean ordinary or overused. Novel means new and original.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, debunk. The other four mean to confirm or prove right. Debunk means to expose as false.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 3 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, obtuse. The other four describe sharp judgment or wisdom. Obtuse means slow to understand.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 1
questions.stem: Critics complained that the report was ______ with errors, finding at least one on almost every page.
questions.explanation: E, replete. An error on almost every page means the report was full of them.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 2
questions.stem: The lack of a visa ______ any possibility of her attending the conference in person.
questions.explanation: C, precluded. Without a visa, attendance is made impossible in advance.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 3
questions.stem: Once the storm had ______, the fishermen went out to inspect the damage to their boats.
questions.explanation: E, abated. They could go out only after the storm had become less intense.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 4
questions.stem: The punishment should be ______ with the offense: a small fine for a small fault, a heavy one for a grave one.
questions.explanation: E, commensurate. Small for small and heavy for grave means in proportion.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 5
questions.stem: Even after losing the first two games, the coach remained ______, insisting that the team would still win the series.
questions.explanation: D, sanguine. Insisting on a win after two losses is optimism in a hard situation.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 6
questions.stem: Plastic bags have become so ______ that they are now found on remote islands and mountain tops.
questions.explanation: B, ubiquitous. Found even in remote places means found everywhere.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 7
questions.stem: To refuse to answer the committee's questions was ______ to an admission of guilt.
questions.explanation: C, tantamount. Tantamount to means equal in effect to.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 8
questions.stem: The new software ______ the need for manual checks, since every error is now caught automatically.
questions.explanation: B, obviated. Automatic checking removes the need for manual checks.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 9
questions.stem: The ______ shopkeeper snapped at customers for the smallest reason.
questions.explanation: D, irascible. Snapping for the smallest reason shows a quick temper.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 10
questions.stem: A ______ of skilled nurses forced the hospital to close two of its wards.
questions.explanation: D, dearth. Wards close when there is a shortage of nurses.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 11
questions.stem: Bad weather ______ the search, and by nightfall the teams had covered only half the area.
questions.explanation: B and C, hindered and hampered. Covering only half the area shows the search was slowed. Expedited and facilitated are opposites.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 12
questions.stem: Public interest in the trial ______ as the weeks went by, and soon the courtroom was half empty.
questions.explanation: C and D, waned and dwindled. A half-empty courtroom shows that interest decreased.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 13
questions.stem: There was a ______ of applicants for the post: more than nine hundred people applied for a single job.
questions.explanation: A and B, glut and plethora. Nine hundred applicants for one job is far more than enough. Dearth and paucity mean shortage.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 14
questions.stem: The ministry used radio and newspapers to ______ the new safety advice to every village.
questions.explanation: B and F, disseminate and propagate. Radio and newspapers are used to spread information widely.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 15
questions.stem: The ______ goalkeeper showed no reaction, whether his team scored or conceded.
questions.explanation: A and F, imperturbable and phlegmatic. Showing no reaction either way means not easily excited or upset.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 16
questions.stem: The ______ old farmer quarreled with every visitor and chased most of them off his land.
questions.explanation: A and E, irascible and cantankerous. Quarreling with everyone shows a bad temper.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 17
questions.stem: On such a ______ income, the family could afford meat only once a month.
questions.explanation: D and F, scant and meager. Affording meat once a month means the income is very small.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 18
questions.stem: The team was ______ after its unexpected victory, singing all the way home.
questions.explanation: D and F, elated and jubilant. Singing after a victory shows great joy.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 19
questions.stem: The editor cut every ______ sentence, keeping only what the argument needed.
questions.explanation: A and B, superfluous and extraneous. What the argument does not need is unnecessary.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 20
questions.stem: The government sent troops to ______ the uprising before it could spread.
questions.explanation: B and E, quell and stifle. Troops are sent to put down an uprising, not to help it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, expedite. The other four mean to slow down or obstruct. Expedite means to speed up.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, meager. The other four suggest large amounts. Meager means small in amount.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: C, augment. The other four mean to decrease. Augment means to increase.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, ebullient. The other four describe gloom. Ebullient means cheerful and full of energy.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 4 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, truncate. The other four mean to spread. Truncate means to cut short.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 1
questions.stem: A lifelong ______, the old writer avoided all company and said that he preferred his dog to any human being.
questions.explanation: B, misanthrope. Someone who dislikes people in general is a misanthrope.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 2
questions.stem: The judge, known for her ______, could not be bribed or flattered into favoring either side.
questions.explanation: E, probity. Being impossible to bribe is complete honesty.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 3
questions.stem: The king was surrounded by ______ who praised his every decision, however foolish.
questions.explanation: B, sycophants. People who praise even foolish decisions are flatterers.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 4
questions.stem: Their ______ meetings took place after midnight in an abandoned warehouse, far from any watching eyes.
questions.explanation: D, clandestine. Meetings held at midnight away from watching eyes are secret.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 5
questions.stem: The assassination of the archduke ______ a war that the great powers had long expected but none had planned for that summer.
questions.explanation: A, precipitated. The event caused the war to break out suddenly.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 6
questions.stem: Security footage ______ the cashier, showing that she had been nowhere near the safe.
questions.explanation: B, exonerated. Proof that she was not there clears her of blame.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 7
questions.stem: The ______ purpose of the trip was research, but the long days at the beach suggested otherwise.
questions.explanation: A, ostensible. The stated purpose seems not to be the real one.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 8
questions.stem: After years in the emergency ward, the nurse had become ______ to sights that would make a newcomer faint.
questions.explanation: E, inured. Long exposure has made her used to unpleasant sights.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 9
questions.stem: Motorists who ______ the new parking rules will have their cars removed.
questions.explanation: A, flout. Cars are removed when drivers openly disobey the rules.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 10
questions.stem: The economist's ______ article, published five years before the crash, described almost exactly how it would unfold.
questions.explanation: A, prescient. Describing the crash five years early is predicting events before they happen.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 11
questions.stem: The ______ assistant agreed with everything the director said and rushed to carry her bags.
questions.explanation: B and D, fawning and obsequious. Agreeing with everything and carrying bags shows too much eagerness to please. Insolent and impudent are opposites.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 12
questions.stem: He has a ______ for exaggeration, so his friends halve every number he quotes.
questions.explanation: A and B, proclivity and propensity. He tends to exaggerate, so the blank means a natural tendency.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 13
questions.stem: The ______ effects of the rumor spread slowly, and its damage was noticed only months later.
questions.explanation: C and F, insidious and pernicious. Harm that spreads slowly and unnoticed is pernicious or insidious.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 14
questions.stem: The signs were ______: with demand rising and costs falling, the launch could hardly have come at a better time.
questions.explanation: D and E, propitious and auspicious. "Could hardly have come at a better time" means the signs were favorable.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 15
questions.stem: He took a ______ glance at his neighbor's answer sheet when the examiner turned away.
questions.explanation: A and E, furtive and surreptitious. A glance taken when the examiner looks away is secret.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 16
questions.stem: The pupil's ______ reply to the head teacher earned him a week of detention.
questions.explanation: B and D, insolent and impudent. A reply that earns detention is rudely disrespectful.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 17
questions.stem: Rival leaders accused foreign agents of trying to ______ rebellion in the border provinces.
questions.explanation: B and F, incite and foment. Agents accused over a rebellion are said to stir it up.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 18
questions.stem: Falling orders ______ a hard winter for the shipyards.
questions.explanation: A and E, portended and presaged. Falling orders are a sign of trouble to come.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 19
questions.stem: She ______ cruelty to animals and would leave the room if anyone joked about it.
questions.explanation: C and F, loathed and abhorred. Leaving the room shows that she hated it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 20
questions.stem: There was a ______ understanding between the neighbors, never put into words, that neither would build above two floors.
questions.explanation: A and C, implicit and tacit. An understanding never put into words is unstated.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: C, aversion. The other four mean a liking or tendency toward something. Aversion means a strong dislike.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: C, insubordinate. The other four mean too eager to obey or please. Insubordinate means refusing to obey.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, overt. The other four mean secret. Overt means done openly.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: D, benevolent. The other four describe wicked or treacherous character. Benevolent means kind.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 5 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: D, absolve. The other four mean to stir up or provoke. Absolve means to free from guilt.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 1
questions.stem: The lecture grew so long that the audience became ______, shifting in their seats and whispering.
questions.explanation: D, restive. Shifting and whispering show restlessness. Disinterested means impartial, not bored.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 2
questions.stem: A referee must be ______, with no reason to prefer one team over the other.
questions.explanation: E, disinterested. Having no reason to prefer either side is being impartial.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 3
questions.stem: A ______ smell from the rotting fish drove the visitors out of the market.
questions.explanation: A, noisome. Rotting fish produce a foul smell, which is what noisome means.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 4
questions.stem: The path up the cliff was ______, doubling back on itself more than thirty times.
questions.explanation: A, tortuous. A path that doubles back many times is full of twists.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 5
questions.stem: He had the ______ to correct the surgeon in the middle of the operation, though he had been a student for only a week.
questions.explanation: B, temerity. A new student correcting a surgeon shows reckless boldness.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 6
questions.stem: The law ______ the sale of fireworks to anyone under eighteen, and shops that ignore it are fined.
questions.explanation: A, proscribes. Shops are fined, so the law forbids the sale.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 7
questions.stem: Although the spider looks dangerous, it is entirely ______ and can safely be picked up.
questions.explanation: D, innocuous. "Although" and "safely" show that the spider is harmless.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 8
questions.stem: Her praise was so ______ that the author suspected she had not read the book at all.
questions.explanation: C, fulsome. Praise so excessive that it seems insincere is fulsome.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 9
questions.stem: Finding that the experiment had been contaminated, the scientist publicly ______ the claim she had made the year before.
questions.explanation: E, recanted. Withdrawing an earlier claim is recanting it.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 10
questions.stem: The essay offered a ______ critique that went straight to the weakest point of the theory.
questions.explanation: E, trenchant. A critique that goes straight to the weak point is sharp and forceful.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 11
questions.stem: Smoking has ______ effects on almost every organ of the body, which is why doctors urge patients to quit.
questions.explanation: A and B, deleterious and detrimental. Doctors urge quitting because the effects are harmful. Salubrious and salutary mean beneficial.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 12
questions.stem: The ______ deserter fled at the first sound of gunfire, leaving his comrades behind.
questions.explanation: A and C, pusillanimous and craven. Fleeing and abandoning comrades is cowardice.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 13
questions.stem: The ______ explorer crossed the ice alone, undeterred by storms or hunger.
questions.explanation: C and F, intrepid and dauntless. Undeterred by storms or hunger means fearless.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 14
questions.stem: His ______ review mocked the play so bitterly that the theater canceled its run.
questions.explanation: C and F, caustic and acerbic. Bitter mockery is caustic or acerbic.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 15
questions.stem: The ______ sign, flashing pink and green, could be seen from three streets away.
questions.explanation: A and E, garish and gaudy. Flashing pink and green is unpleasantly bright and showy.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 16
questions.stem: His ______ behavior at dinner, shouting across the table and insulting the cook, embarrassed his hosts.
questions.explanation: A and D, boorish and uncouth. Shouting and insulting the cook is rude and ill-mannered. Urbane and suave are opposites.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 17
questions.stem: The march through the swamp was ______, and several soldiers collapsed from exhaustion.
questions.explanation: A and F, arduous and laborious. Soldiers collapsing from exhaustion shows that it needed great effort.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 18
questions.stem: Once deceived by a partner, she was ______ of signing any agreement without a lawyer present.
questions.explanation: B and E, wary and chary. Past deception has made her cautious.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 19
questions.stem: The coach's half-time ______ against lazy defending could be heard outside the stadium.
questions.explanation: A and D, tirade and harangue. A loud speech against something is an angry attack. Eulogy and panegyric are speeches of praise.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 20
questions.stem: Engineers concluded that a tunnel under the bay was not ______, since the rock was too soft to hold.
questions.explanation: A and B, viable and feasible. Rock too soft to hold means the tunnel cannot be built.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 21
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: E, salubrious. The other four mean harmful. Salubrious means good for health.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 22
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, timorous. The other four mean bold or fearless. Timorous means easily frightened.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 23
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, understated. The other four mean showy. Understated means quiet and restrained.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 24
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: A, panegyric. The other four are verbal attacks. A panegyric is a speech of praise.

questions.label: Vocab Quiz Week 6 · 25
questions.stem: Four of the five words are close in meaning. Which word does not belong?
questions.explanation: B, urbane. The other four mean rude or crude. Urbane means polished and well-mannered.
